Existence: for each y in V the linear functional x -> beta(bx, y) on V is represented uniquely as x -> beta(x, w_y) for some w_y in V, by nondegeneracy of beta in the second variable (the map w -> (x -> beta(x, w)) is an isomorphism V -> V^*); the map y -> w_y is K-linear, and b^dag := (y -> w_y) satisfies the defining identity. Uniqueness: if beta(x, Ay) = beta(x, By) for all x, y, then beta(x, (A - B)y) = 0 for all x; nondegeneracy in the first variable (for w != 0 there exists x with beta(x, w) != 0) forces (A - B)y = 0 for all y, hence A = B. The adjoint is K-linear: applying the defining identity to b + c gives beta((b+c)x, y) = beta(x, b^dag y) + beta(x, c^dag y) = beta(x, (b^dag + c^dag) y), so (b+c)^dag = b^dag + c^dag; applying it to (lambda) b gives ((lambda) b)^dag = (lambda) b^dag.

Step 3 (U^dag = U^{-1}). We show beta(Ux, y) = beta(x, U^{-1} y) for all x, y in V, and then invoke uniqueness of the adjoint. Given x, y in V, put z = U^{-1} y, so y = U z. By the isometry hypothesis beta(Ux, Uy) = beta(x, y) applied to the pair (x, z), we have beta(Ux, y) = beta(Ux, U z) = beta(x, z) = beta(x, U^{-1} y). Hence beta(Ux, y) = beta(x, U^{-1} y) for all x, y, so U^dag = U^{-1}.

Step 4 (N^dag = U^{-1} - 1). By K-linearity of the adjoint and Step 3, N^dag = (U - 1)^dag = U^dag - 1^dag = U^{-1} - 1, where 1^dag = 1 because beta(1 x, y) = beta(x, y) = beta(x, 1 y) for all x, y.

Step 5 (N N^dag is nilpotent). Compute N N^dag = (U - 1)(U^{-1} - 1) = U U^{-1} - U - U^{-1} + 1 = 2 - U - U^{-1}. We claim 2 - U - U^{-1} = -N^2 U^{-1}: indeed -N^2 U^{-1} = -(U - 1)^2 U^{-1} = -(U^2 - 2U + 1) U^{-1} = -U + 2 - U^{-1} = 2 - U - U^{-1}. So N N^dag = -N^2 U^{-1}. Let r >= 1 be the index of nilpotence of N, so N^r = 0 and N^{r-1} != 0. Since U = 1 + N, the finite geometric series (valid because N^r = 0) gives U^{-1} = 1 - N + N^2 - ... + (-1)^{r-1} N^{r-1}. Therefore N N^dag = -N^2 U^{-1} = -N^2 + N^3 - ... + (-1)^r N^{r+1}, in which every term N^j with j >= r is zero. Thus N N^dag is a polynomial in N with zero constant term (in fact divisible by N^2). Since N is nilpotent, every polynomial in N with zero constant term is nilpotent; hence N N^dag is nilpotent.

Step 6 (a nilpotent endomorphism has trace 0). Let M be a nilpotent endomorphism of V, so M^s = 0 for some s >= 1. Over an algebraic closure K' of K, the only eigenvalue of M is 0: if (lambda) v = M v with v != 0, then 0 = M^s v = (lambda)^s v forces (lambda)^s = 0, hence (lambda) = 0. The characteristic polynomial of M is the product of (t - (lambda_i)) over its eigenvalues with multiplicity, so it equals (t)^{dim_K V}. The trace of M is the negative of the coefficient of (t)^{dim_K V - 1} in the characteristic polynomial, which is 0. Hence Tr_V(M) = 0. Applying this to M = N N^dag (nilpotent by Step 5), we get Tr_V(N N^dag) = 0.

Step 7 (contradiction). The hypothesis states that Tr_V(b b^dag) != 0 for every nonzero b in K[F]. Since N != 0 and N in K[F], it applies to b = N, giving Tr_V(N N^dag) != 0. This contradicts Step 6, which gives Tr_V(N N^dag) = 0.

Therefore U = 1."
\}

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let F be an element of GL_K(V), let A be an F-stable subspace of V, let C=V/A, and let F_C be the induced operator on C. If F|_A and F_C are semisimple over an algebraic closure of K and their spectra in that algebraic closure are disjoint, then F is semisimple on V.
proof: Let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K. Put Vbar = V tensor_K Kbar, Abar = A tensor_K Kbar, and identify Cbar = C tensor_K Kbar with Vbar/Abar. Let Fbar be the induced endomorphism of Vbar. Then Fbar restricted to Abar is F|_A tensor 1, and it induces F_C tensor 1 on Cbar. Let Lambda be the spectrum of F|_A tensor 1 in Kbar and Mu the spectrum of F_C tensor 1 in Kbar; by hypothesis Lambda and Mu are disjoint. Since both operators are semisimple over Kbar, their minimal polynomials are m_A(t)=prod_{lambda in Lambda}(t-lambda) and m_C(t)=prod_{mu in Mu}(t-mu), with the convention that the product over an empty set is 1 (this is the minimal polynomial of the zero operator on the zero space). Because the two sets of roots are disjoint, m_A and m_C are coprime in Kbar[t]. Hence there exist u,v in Kbar[t] with u m_A + v m_C = 1. Define P = v(Fbar) m_C(Fbar) in End_Kbar(Vbar). For a in Abar, m_A(F|_A tensor 1)a = 0, so P a = (v(F|_A tensor 1) m_C(F|_A tensor 1)) a = (1 - u(F|_A tensor 1) m_A(F|_A tensor 1)) a = a. Let q: Vbar -> Cbar be the quotient map. For x in Vbar, q(P x) = v(F_C tensor 1) m_C(F_C tensor 1) q(x) = 0, so P x is in Abar. Thus im P is contained in Abar and P|_Abar = id; consequently im P = Abar and P^2 = P. Let Bbar = ker P. Then Vbar = Abar direct sum Bbar. Since P is a polynomial in Fbar, it commutes with Fbar, so Bbar is Fbar-stable. The restriction q|_Bbar: Bbar -> Cbar is an isomorphism of Fbar-modules. Indeed, if b in Bbar and q(b)=0, then b in Abar, hence b = P b = 0. Conversely, for any x in Vbar, x - P x is in Bbar and q(x - P x) = q(x), so q|_Bbar is surjective. It is equivariant because q(Fbar b) = (F_C tensor 1) q(b) for b in Bbar. Therefore Fbar|_Bbar is isomorphic to F_C tensor 1 and is semisimple. Thus Fbar is the direct sum of the semisimple operators F|_A tensor 1 on Abar and Fbar|_Bbar on Bbar. Choosing a basis of eigenvectors for each summand and taking their union gives a basis of eigenvectors of Fbar on Vbar; hence Fbar is semisimple. It remains to note that this is equivalent to F being semisimple over K. Let m in K[t] be the minimal polynomial of F. Since Fbar is semisimple, its minimal polynomial over Kbar is mbar = prod_{lambda in S}(t-lambda), where S is the set of eigenvalues of Fbar. Since K has characteristic 0, Kbar/K is Galois; the set S is stable under Gal(Kbar/K), because Fbar is defined over K; hence mbar is in K[t]. It annihilates F, so m divides mbar in K[t]. Since mbar is squarefree, m is squarefree. Write m = prod_{i=1}^r f_i with distinct monic irreducible polynomials f_i. By the Chinese remainder theorem, K[t]/(m) is isomorphic to the direct sum of the fields K[t]/(f_i); the corresponding idempotents act on V as projections onto ker f_i(F), so V = direct sum_{i=1}^r ker f_i(F). On W_i = ker f_i(F), the relation f_i(F)=0 makes W_i a vector space over the field K[t]/(f_i); choosing a basis over that field shows that W_i is a direct sum of copies of the simple K[t]-module K[t]/(f_i). Hence F is semisimple on each W_i, and therefore on V. This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^d=H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor class, L cup product with xi, and P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d, and beta the Poincare pairing on H^d. Suppose F preserves P^d, beta|_{P^d} is nondegenerate, beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) on P^d, and for every nonzero x in P^d some n>=1 satisfies beta(x,F^n x)+(-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x,F^{-n} x)!=0. If U is the unipotent part of F|_{P^d}, then U is the identity.
proof: Let V=P^d and K=Q_ell. By the standard finiteness theorem for etale cohomology of smooth projective varieties over finite fields, H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) is finite dimensional over K, so V is a finite dimensional K-vector space. If V=0, the unipotent part of F|_V is the identity and there is nothing to prove. Now write F_V=F|_V. Since F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, it is an automorphism of H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), and because F preserves V, F_V is an automorphism of V with inverse F_V^{-1}=F^{-1}|_V. The Poincare pairing beta is the Q_ell-valued form obtained from the trace pairing (x,y)->tr_X(x cup y) by the chosen identification of the Tate twist with Q_ell. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_469, applied with the finite field F_{q^m} and with n=d, we have tr_X(x cup y)=(-1)^{d(2d-d)} tr_X(y cup x)=(-1)^{d^2} tr_X(y cup x)=(-1)^d tr_X(y cup x) for all x,y in H^d. Since the identification of the Tate twist with Q_ell is Q_ell-linear, the Q_ell-valued pairing beta satisfies beta(y,x)=(-1)^d beta(x,y) for all x,y in H^d. Hence beta_V=beta|_{V x V} is nondegenerate by hypothesis and satisfies beta_V(x,y)=epsilon beta_V(y,x) with epsilon=(-1)^d. The hypothesis beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) on P^d becomes beta_V(F_V x,F_V y)=c beta_V(x,y) for all x,y in V, where c=q^{md} is a nonzero element of K. Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/e86395 to K, V, epsilon, beta_V, F_V, c, and U, the unipotent part of F_V. For every integer n>=1 the lemma defines G_n(x,y)=beta_V(x,F_V^n y)+epsilon c^n beta_V(x,F_V^{-n} y). Because epsilon c^n=(-1)^d (q^{md})^n=(-1)^d q^{mdn}, this is exactly the form beta(x,F^n y)+(-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x,F^{-n} y) on P^d. The lemma gives G_n(Ux,Uy)=G_n(x,y) for all x,y in V and all n>=1. The assumed condition says that for every nonzero x in V there exists n>=1 such that beta(x,F^n x)+(-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x,F^{-n} x) != 0, i.e. G_n(x,x) != 0. Finally apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/452e8b to the unipotent automorphism U of V and the family (G_n)_{n>=1}. It follows that U is the identity on V, i.e. on P^d.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^d=H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor class, L cup product with xi, and P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d, and beta the Poincare pairing on H^d. Suppose F preserves P^d, beta|_{P^d} is nondegenerate, and beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) on P^d. For n>=1 put G_n(x,y)=beta(x,F^n y)+(-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x,F^{-n} y) on P^d. Then the set of x in P^d such that G_n(x,y)=0 for every y in P^d is the kernel of q^{mdn}F^{-n}+(-1)^d F^n on P^d.
proof:
That lemma concerns the unipotent part and is not needed for my argument. My proof is fully self-contained linear algebra relying only on the target's own hypotheses, so no lemma or reference is cited.

\{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/d14860",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let V := P^d, the Q_ell-subspace of H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) cut out by L = cup product with xi, i.e. V = ker(L: H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Because X is a smooth projective variety over the finite field F_{q^m}, the etale cohomology group H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) is a finite-dimensional vector space over Q_ell (standard finite-dimensionality theorem for etale cohomology: for a smooth projective variety over a finite field each H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell, being the Q_ell-ification of a finitely generated Z_ell-module). Hence V, a Q_ell-subspace of a finite-dimensional space, is itself finite-dimensional over Q_ell.

Let beta: V x V -> Q_ell be the restriction of the Poincare pairing to V. By hypothesis beta is nondegenerate on V. Let F: V -> V be the restriction of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius to V; this is well-defined because F preserves P^d = V. By hypothesis,
    (H)  beta(Fx, Fy) = q^{md} beta(x, y)  for all x, y in V.
Set c := q^{md} in Q_ell. Since q = p^a >= 2 and m, d >= 1, and Q_ell has characteristic 0, c is a nonzero element of Q_ell, i.e. c in Q_ell^*.

Step 1 (F is invertible on V). Suppose Fx = 0 for some x in V. Then for every y in V, by (H),
    c beta(x, y) = beta(Fx, Fy) = beta(0, Fy) = 0.
Since c != 0, beta(x, y) = 0 for every y in V. By nondegeneracy of beta (in the first variable), x = 0. Thus ker(F) = 0, so F is injective. As V is finite-dimensional, an injective endomorphism of V is surjective, hence F is invertible. Let F^{-1} denote the inverse of F on V, and write F^n, F^{-n} for the iterates.

Step 2 (adjoint of F and the basic identity). Because beta is nondegenerate and V is finite-dimensional, the map V -> V^*, w -> (y -> beta(w, y)), is an isomorphism; consequently every Q_ell-linear endomorphism T of V has a unique adjoint T^*: V -> V characterized by beta(Tx, y) = beta(x, T^* y) for all x, y in V (for fixed x the functional y -> beta(Tx, y) corresponds to a unique T^* x, and x -> T^* x is linear).

Compute F^* F. For all x, y in V,
    beta(x, F^*(Fy)) = beta(Fx, Fy)      [definition of the adjoint with T = F]
                     = c beta(x, y)      [by (H)]
                     = beta(x, c y).
By nondegeneracy of beta in the first variable (beta(x, w) = 0 for all x in V forces w = 0), we obtain F^* F = c I_V. Since F is invertible (Step 1), multiplying on the right by F^{-1} gives F^* = c F^{-1}.

Now for all x, y in V, by the definition of the adjoint and F^* = c F^{-1},
    (1)  beta(Fx, y) = beta(x, F^* y) = beta(x, c F^{-1} y) = c beta(x, F^{-1} y).
(Equivalently, (1) also follows directly from (H) by substituting u = F^{-1}x, v = F^{-1}y, which gives beta(x, y) = c beta(F^{-1}x, F^{-1}y), and then replacing x by Fx.)

Step 3 (identities for all powers). We prove by induction on n >= 1 that for all x, y in V:
    (2)  beta(x, F^n y) = c^n beta(F^{-n} x, y),
    (3)  beta(x, F^{-n} y) = c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y).

Proof of (2). Base n = 1: write x = F u with u = F^{-1} x. Then
    beta(x, Fy) = beta(Fu, Fy) = c beta(u, y) = c beta(F^{-1} x, y) = c^1 beta(F^{-1} x, y),
where the third equality uses (H). So (2) holds for n = 1.
Inductive step: assume (2) for n - 1 (n >= 2). Write x = F u with u = F^{-1} x. Then
    beta(x, F^n y) = beta(Fu, F^n y)
                   = beta(u, F^*(F^n y))        [adjoint definition]
                   = beta(u, c F^{-1} F^n y)    [since F^* = c F^{-1}]
                   = c beta(u, F^{n-1} y)
                   = c beta(F^{-1} x, F^{n-1} y)
                   = c * c^{n-1} beta(F^{-(n-1)} F^{-1} x, y)   [induction hypothesis on (u, F^{n-1} y)]
                   = c^n beta(F^{-n} x, y).
So (2) holds for n.

Proof of (3). Base n = 1: from (1), beta(Fx, y) = c beta(x, F^{-1} y), hence beta(x, F^{-1} y) = c^{-1} beta(Fx, y) = c^{-1} beta(F^1 x, y). So (3) holds for n = 1.
Inductive step: assume (3) for n - 1 (n >= 2). Applying (1) with the second argument equal to F^{-(n-1)} y gives beta(Fx, F^{-(n-1)} y) = c beta(x, F^{-1} F^{-(n-1)} y) = c beta(x, F^{-n} y), i.e.
    beta(x, F^{-n} y) = c^{-1} beta(Fx, F^{-(n-1)} y).
Now apply the induction hypothesis (3) to the pair (Fx, F^{-(n-1)} y):
    beta(Fx, F^{-(n-1)} y) = c^{-(n-1)} beta(F^{n-1} (Fx), y) = c^{-(n-1)} beta(F^n x, y).
Therefore
    beta(x, F^{-n} y) = c^{-1} * c^{-(n-1)} beta(F^n x, y) = c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y).
So (3) holds for n.

Step 4 (rewrite G_n). Fix n >= 1. For all x, y in V, using (2) and (3),
    G_n(x, y) = beta(x, F^n y) + (-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x, F^{-n} y)
              = c^n beta(F^{-n} x, y) + (-1)^d q^{mdn} c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y).
Since c = q^{md}, we have c^n = q^{mdn} and c^{-n} = q^{-mdn}. Substituting these values,
    G_n(x, y) = q^{mdn} beta(F^{-n} x, y) + (-1)^d q^{mdn} q^{-mdn} beta(F^n x, y)
              = q^{mdn} beta(F^{-n} x, y) + (-1)^d beta(F^n x, y)
              = beta(q^{mdn} F^{-n} x, y) + beta((-1)^d F^n x, y)      [bilinearity of beta]
              = beta((q^{mdn} F^{-n} + (-1)^d F^n) x, y).              (4)

Step 5 (identify the radical). Let T := q^{mdn} F^{-n} + (-1)^d F^n. This is a well-defined Q_ell-linear endomorphism of V because F is invertible, so F^{-n} = (F^{-1})^n is a well-defined endomorphism of V, and q^{mdn}, (-1)^d are scalars in Q_ell. The set appearing in the conclusion is
    R = { x in V : G_n(x, y) = 0 for every y in V }.
By (4),
    R = { x in V : beta(T x, y) = 0 for every y in V }.
By nondegeneracy of beta in the first variable, beta(w, y) = 0 for all y in V if and only if w = 0. Hence
    R = { x in V : T x = 0 } = ker(T) = ker(q^{mdn} F^{-n} + (-1)^d F^n).

This is exactly the stated conclusion. QED.

(Consistency check with the verifier's example: d = 1, q = 4, m = 1, V = Q_ell one-dimensional, beta(x,y) = xy, F = 2I. Then c = 4, G_1(x,y) = beta(x,2y) - 4 beta(x,(1/2)y) = 2xy - 2xy = 0, so R = V; and ker(q^{mdn} F^{-n} + (-1)^d F^n) = ker(4 * (1/2) I - 2 I) = ker(0) = V, in agreement.)"
\}

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=1, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, let U=X\Y, and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then the localization segment H_c^d_et(U_k,Q_ell) -> H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^d_et(Y_k,Q_ell) -> H_c^{d+1}_et(U_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) with the usual maps is an exact sequence of F-modules.
proof: Set Q=q^m. Then Q=p^{am} is a prime power and k=overline F_q=overline F_Q. Let j:U->X be the open immersion and i:Y->X the closed immersion. The notation Y subset X means that Y is the effective Cartier divisor corresponding to the closed subscheme; its associated line bundle is ample by hypothesis. An effective Cartier divisor in a scheme of pure dimension d has pure dimension d-1, and smoothness is assumed, so Y is an effective ample divisor, smooth of pure dimension d-1. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type, for the closed immersion i and the complementary open immersion j there is the standard localization long exact sequence ... -> H^n_c(U_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) -> H^{n+1}_c(U_k,Q_ell) -> ... whose middle map is i^* and whose other maps are the usual extension-by-zero and connecting maps. Now apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283 to X over F_Q, the effective ample divisor Y, and the prime ell != p = char(F_Q). It gives the localization long exact sequence of finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces for this pair, with middle map i^*, and it asserts that every map in this sequence commutes with the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of the terms. Taking n=d gives the five-term segment A=H_c^d(U_k,Q_ell) -> B=H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> C=H^d_et(Y_k,Q_ell) -> D=H_c^{d+1}(U_k,Q_ell) -> E=H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) with the usual maps. Since the long exact sequence is exact at every term, its restriction to this contiguous segment is exact at the three internal terms: im(A->B)=ker(B->C), im(B->C)=ker(C->D), and im(C->D)=ker(D->E). Finally, let F denote the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on each of A,B,C,D,E (with F understood on the relevant term). By the Frobenius equivariance in Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283, each of the four maps f in the segment satisfies f(Fv)=F(f(v)) for all v in its source. Thus each map is a homomorphism of F-modules, i.e. a Q_ell-linear map commuting with the distinguished Frobenius automorphism, and the kernels and images appearing above are F-stable. Hence the equalities above hold in the category of F-modules, so the segment is an exact sequence of F-modules.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be either 1 or -1, let beta: V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F be an element of GL_K(V), let c be a nonzero element of K, and let n>=1. Put G_n(x,y)=beta(x,F^n y)+epsilon c^n beta(x,F^{-n} y). Then, if G_n is the zero bilinear form, F is semisimple over an algebraic closure of K.
proof:
Assume that G_n is the zero bilinear form, i.e. G_n(x,y) = 0 for all x, y in V.

Step 1: Derive (F^n)^2 = -epsilon c^n I_V.

Fix y in V. For every x in V, by bilinearity of beta in the second variable,
  0 = G_n(x,y) = beta(x, F^n y) + epsilon c^n beta(x, F^{-n} y) = beta(x, F^n y + epsilon c^n F^{-n} y).
Thus the vector z_y := F^n y + epsilon c^n F^{-n} y satisfies beta(x, z_y) = 0 for every x in V. Since beta is nondegenerate (its left radical is trivial: if beta(x, z) = 0 for all x in V then z = 0), we conclude z_y = 0, i.e.
  F^n y + epsilon c^n F^{-n} y = 0  for every y in V.
Applying F^n to both sides (and using F^n F^{-n} = I_V) gives
  (F^n)^2 y + epsilon c^n y = 0  for every y in V,
hence as an operator identity
  (F^n)^2 = -epsilon c^n I_V.                                    (1)

Step 2: The polynomial P(T) = T^2 + epsilon c^n is squarefree in K[T].

Since char K = 0 and c != 0, we have c^n != 0 and hence epsilon c^n != 0. The discriminant of P is
  disc(P) = 0^2 - 4(epsilon c^n) = -4 epsilon c^n.
In characteristic 0, -4 != 0, and epsilon c^n != 0, so disc(P) != 0. A polynomial over a field is squarefree if and only if it is coprime to its formal derivative (equivalently, it has no repeated root over an algebraic closure). Here P'(T) = 2T, and gcd(P, P') = 1 because P(0) = epsilon c^n != 0 (so T does not divide P). Hence P is squarefree in K[T].

Step 3: F^n is semisimple over an algebraic closure Kbar of K.

By (1), P(F^n) = (F^n)^2 + epsilon c^n I_V = 0, so the minimal polynomial mu_{F^n}(T) of F^n over K divides P(T) in K[T]. Since P is squarefree, every divisor of P in K[T] is also squarefree; in particular mu_{F^n} is squarefree in K[T]. Passing to Kbar, each irreducible factor of mu_{F^n} (which is squarefree over K) splits into distinct linear factors over Kbar, and distinct irreducible factors over K have no common root over Kbar. Therefore mu_{F^n} splits over Kbar into a product of distinct linear factors. An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over a field is diagonalizable over an algebraic closure if and only if its minimal polynomial over that algebraic closure splits into distinct linear factors; hence F^n is semisimple (diagonalizable) over Kbar.

Step 4: F is semisimple over Kbar.

We now apply the following standard linear-algebra result (proved as lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/896297): Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be an invertible K-linear operator on V, and let r >= 1 be an integer. If T^r is semisimple on V (equivalently, diagonalizable over an algebraic closure of K), then T is semisimple on V.

Taking T = F, r = n, and noting that F in GL_K(V) is invertible and char K = 0, Step 3 gives that F^n is semisimple over Kbar. By the cited lemma, F is semisimple over Kbar.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a subfield of C, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be a K-linear endomorphism of V, let W be a T-stable K-subspace of V, and let q>0 be a real number. If every root in C of the characteristic polynomial of T has absolute value q, then every root in C of the characteristic polynomial of the restriction of T to W has absolute value q.
proof:
Let n = dim_K V and r = dim_K W, with 0 <= r <= n. If r = 0, then W = {0}, the restriction T|_W is the zero endomorphism of the zero space, its characteristic polynomial is the constant polynomial 1, which has no roots in C, and the assertion is vacuous. Hence assume r >= 1 (the argument below is in fact valid for all r, including r = n, in which case W = V and there is nothing to prove).

Step 1 (block upper triangular form). Choose a K-basis e_1, ..., e_r of W and extend it to a K-basis e_1, ..., e_n of V (every basis of a subspace extends to a basis of the ambient space). For i = 1, ..., n write T e_i = sum_{j=1}^n a_{j i} e_j. Since W is T-stable, for i <= r the vector T e_i lies in W, so a_{j i} = 0 for all j > r. Thus the n x n matrix M = (a_{j i}) of T in the basis (e_i) is block upper triangular:
  M = [ A   B ]
      [ 0   C ],
where A = (a_{j i})_{1<=i,j<=r} is the r x r matrix of the restriction T|_W in the basis (e_1, ..., e_r) of W, and C is the (n-r) x (n-r) matrix of the induced endomorphism Tbar: V/W -> V/W, Tbar(v + W) = T v + W, in the basis (e_{r+1} + W, ..., e_n + W) of V/W. Indeed, for j > r, T e_j = sum_{i=r+1}^n a_{i j} e_i + (a linear combination of e_1,...,e_r), so Tbar(e_j + W) = sum_{i=r+1}^n a_{i j} (e_i + W).

Step 2 (determinant of a block upper triangular matrix, proved explicitly). Let N = [P  Q; 0  R] be any block matrix with P an r x r matrix, R an (n-r) x (n-r) matrix, and 0 the zero (n-r) x r block, with entries in C. By the Leibniz formula, det N = sum_{sigma in S_n} sgn(sigma) prod_{i=1}^n N_{i sigma(i)}. For a given permutation sigma, if sigma(j) <= r for some j > r, then the factor N_{j sigma(j)} is an entry of the zero block, hence equals 0, and the term for sigma vanishes. Therefore only permutations sigma with sigma({r+1, ..., n}) subset {r+1, ..., n} contribute; since sigma is bijective, this is equivalent to sigma({1, ..., r}) = {1, ..., r} and sigma({r+1, ..., n}) = {r+1, ..., n}. Any such sigma decomposes uniquely as a pair (sigma_1, sigma_2) with sigma_1 in S_r and sigma_2 in S_{n-r}, with sgn(sigma) = sgn(sigma_1) sgn(sigma_2) and prod_{i=1}^n N_{i sigma(i)} = (prod_{i=1}^r N_{i sigma_1(i)}) (prod_{i=r+1}^n N_{i sigma_2(i)}). Summing over all such sigma, the double sum factors as a product of two independent sums, giving det N = (sum_{sigma_1 in S_r} sgn(sigma_1) prod_{i=1}^r N_{i sigma_1(i)}) (sum_{sigma_2 in S_{n-r}} sgn(sigma_2) prod_{i=r+1}^n N_{i sigma_2(i)}) = det P * det R.

Step 3 (factorization of the characteristic polynomial). For lambda in C, the matrix lambda I_n - M has the block form [lambda I_r - A, -B; 0, lambda I_{n-r} - C], so by Step 2,
  det(lambda I_n - M) = det(lambda I_r - A) * det(lambda I_{n-r} - C).
Since A is the matrix of T|_W in a basis of W and C is the matrix of Tbar in a basis of V/W, the left side is the characteristic polynomial chi_T(lambda) of T, the first factor is the characteristic polynomial chi_{T|_W}(lambda) of T|_W, and the second is the characteristic polynomial chi_{Tbar}(lambda) of Tbar. Hence, as an identity of polynomials in C[lambda],
  chi_T(lambda) = chi_{T|_W}(lambda) * chi_{Tbar}(lambda).

Step 4 (conclusion). Let alpha in C be a root of chi_{T|_W}, i.e. chi_{T|_W}(alpha) = 0. By the identity of Step 3, chi_T(alpha) = chi_{T|_W}(alpha) chi_{Tbar}(alpha) = 0, so alpha is a root in C of the characteristic polynomial of T. By hypothesis, every root in C of chi_T has absolute value q; therefore |alpha| = q. Since alpha was an arbitrary root in C of chi_{T|_W}, every such root has absolute value q, as required. This completes the proof, including the degenerate case r = 0 handled at the start.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let d>=1, let V=direct sum_{r=0}^{2d} V^r be a finite-dimensional graded K-vector space, and let L:V^r -> V^{r+2} be K-linear for 0<=r<=2d-2 such that L^{d-n}:V^n -> V^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. Put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:V^r -> V^{2d-r+2}) for 0<=r<=d. Let F be a K-linear automorphism of V preserving each V^r and commuting with L. If F is semisimple on L^k(P^{d-2k}) for every 0<=k<=floor(d/2), then F is semisimple on V^d.
proof:
We prove the result in three steps. Write V^r for the r-th graded piece, so V = ⊕_{r=0}^{2d} V^r, and recall that L: V^r -> V^{r+2} is K-linear for 0 <= r <= 2d-2 with L^{d-n}: V^n -> V^{2d-n} an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d; P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}: V^r -> V^{2d-r+2}) for 0 <= r <= d; and F is a K-linear automorphism of V preserving each V^r and commuting with L. Note first that for s >= 2d the space V^s is 0 (the grading stops at 2d).

Step 1 (Lefschetz decomposition). We claim that for every r with 0 <= r <= d,
  V^r = ⊕_{k=0}^{floor(r/2)} L^k(P^{r-2k})
as a direct sum of subspaces of V^r. In particular, for r = d,
  V^d = ⊕_{k=0}^{floor(d/2)} L^k(P^{d-2k}).
We prove the claim by induction on r.

Base, r = 0: P^0 = ker(L^{d+1}: V^0 -> V^{2d+2}). Since V^{2d+2} = 0, the map L^{d+1} is the zero map, so P^0 = V^0. Thus V^0 = P^0, the k=0 term.
Base, r = 1: P^1 = ker(L^{d}: V^1 -> V^{2d+1}). Since V^{2d+1} = 0, L^{d} = 0 and P^1 = V^1. Thus V^1 = P^1, the k=0 term.

Inductive step. Let 2 <= r <= d and assume the claim for r-2, i.e. V^{r-2} = ⊕_{j=0}^{floor((r-2)/2)} L^j(P^{r-2-2j}). We prove V^r = P^r ⊕ L(V^{r-2}), where L(V^{r-2}) := im(L: V^{r-2} -> V^r).

(1) P^r ∩ L(V^{r-2}) = {0}. Let x ∈ P^r ∩ L(V^{r-2}) and write x = L y with y ∈ V^{r-2}. Since x ∈ P^r, L^{d-r+1} x = 0, hence L^{d-r+2} y = L^{d-r+1}(L y) = 0. By the hypothesis applied with n = r-2 (valid since 0 <= r-2 <= d), L^{d-r+2}: V^{r-2} -> V^{2d-r+2} is an isomorphism; therefore y = 0 and x = 0.

(2) dim_K P^r + dim_K L(V^{r-2}) = dim_K V^r. By rank-nullity applied to L^{d-r+1}: V^r -> V^{2d-r+2},
  dim P^r = dim V^r - dim im(L^{d-r+1}: V^r -> V^{2d-r+2}).
Write L^{d-r+1} = L_{2d-r} ∘ L^{d-r}, where L^{d-r}: V^r -> V^{2d-r} is an isomorphism (hypothesis, n = r) and L_{2d-r}: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}. Since L^{d-r} is surjective, im(L^{d-r+1}) = im(L_{2d-r}: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}). Hence
  dim P^r = dim V^r - dim im(L: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}).
By rank-nullity applied to L: V^{r-2} -> V^r,
  dim L(V^{r-2}) = dim V^{r-2} - dim ker(L: V^{r-2} -> V^r).
Now factor the isomorphism L^{d-r+2}: V^{r-2} -> V^{2d-r+2} (hypothesis, n = r-2) as L^{d-r+2} = L_{2d-r} ∘ L^{d-r+1}, with L^{d-r+1}: V^{r-2} -> V^{2d-r} and L_{2d-r}: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}.
  (a) L_{2d-r}: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2} is surjective, being the second factor of the surjective composition L^{d-r+2} = L_{2d-r} ∘ L^{d-r+1}. Hence im(L: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}) = V^{2d-r+2}, so dim im(L: V^{2d-r} -> V^{2d-r+2}) = dim V^{2d-r+2}.
  (b) L^{d-r+1}: V^{r-2} -> V^{2d-r} is injective, being the first factor of the injective composition L^{d-r+2} = L_{2d-r} ∘ L^{d-r+1}. The map L^{d-r+1} is itself a composition whose rightmost (first-applied) factor is L: V^{r-2} -> V^r (the spaces run V^{r-2} -> V^r -> V^{r+2} -> ... -> V^{2d-r}); a composition is injective only if its first factor is injective, so L: V^{r-2} -> V^r is injective, i.e. dim ker(L: V^{r-2} -> V^r) = 0.
  (c) By the hypothesis with n = r-2, L^{d-r+2}: V^{r-2} -> V^{2d-r+2} is an isomorphism, so dim V^{r-2} = dim V^{2d-r+2}.
Substituting (a), (b), (c):
  dim P^r + dim L(V^{r-2}) = (dim V^r - dim V^{2d-r+2}) + (dim V^{r-2} - 0) = dim V^r - dim V^{2d-r+2} + dim V^{2d-r+2} = dim V^r.
From (1) and (2), V^r = P^r ⊕ L(V^{r-2}).

Finally, L: V^{r-2} -> V^r is injective (part (b)), so it carries the direct sum V^{r-2} = ⊕_j L^j(P^{r-2-2j}) to the direct sum L(V^{r-2}) = ⊕_j L^{j+1}(P^{r-2-2j}) (an injective map sends a direct sum to a direct sum: if ∑_j l_j = 0 with l_j ∈ L(A_j), then l_j = L(a_j) and 0 = L(∑_j a_j) forces ∑_j a_j = 0, hence each a_j = 0 by directness, hence each l_j = 0). Therefore
  V^r = P^r ⊕ ⊕_{j=0}^{floor((r-2)/2)} L^{j+1}(P^{r-2-2j}) = ⊕_{k=0}^{floor(r/2)} L^k(P^{r-2k}),
completing the induction and the claim.

Step 2 (F preserves each summand). Fix 0 <= k <= floor(d/2) and set W_k := L^k(P^{d-2k}). We show F(W_k) = W_k.
First, for each 0 <= s <= d, F(P^s) = P^s. Indeed, P^s = ker(L^{d-s+1}: V^s -> V^{2d-s+2}). Since F preserves V^s and commutes with L (hence with L^{d-s+1}), for x ∈ V^s:
  x ∈ P^s  ⟺  L^{d-s+1} x = 0  ⟺  L^{d-s+1} F x = F(L^{d-s+1} x) = F(0) = 0  ⟺  F x ∈ P^s,
where the middle equivalence uses F ∘ L^{d-s+1} = L^{d-s+1} ∘ F. Because F|_{V^s}: V^s -> V^s is an automorphism (F is invertible and preserves V^s), F(P^s) = P^s.
Then, again using F ∘ L^k = L^k ∘ F,
  F(W_k) = F(L^k(P^{d-2k})) = L^k(F(P^{d-2k})) = L^k(P^{d-2k}) = W_k.
So F preserves each W_k.

Step 3 (Conclusion). By Step 1, V^d = ⊕_{k=0}^{floor(d/2)} W_k is a direct sum. By Step 2, F preserves each W_k, so with respect to this decomposition F is block-diagonal, its k-th block being F|_{W_k}: W_k -> W_k. By hypothesis, each F|_{W_k} is semisimple. A block-diagonal operator is semisimple if and only if each diagonal block is semisimple: after extending scalars to an algebraic closure of K (which does not change semisimplicity, K having characteristic 0), the minimal polynomial of F is the least common multiple of the minimal polynomials of the blocks, and this is a product of distinct linear factors if and only if each block's minimal polynomial is a product of distinct linear factors. Since every block F|_{W_k} is semisimple, F is semisimple on V^d. ∎

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(-d), let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi from H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) to H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell), and let tr_X: H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace. Define beta(x,y)=tr_X(Lx cup y) for x,y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell). Then the set of x in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) for which beta(x,y)=0 for every y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is equal to ker(L).
proof:
Let V := H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) and W := H^{d+1}_et(X_k, Q_ell). Let e denote the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(-d). Define the left radical of beta by
R := { x in V : beta(x,y) = 0 for every y in V },  where beta(x,y) := tr_X(Lx cup y).
We prove R = ker(L).

Step 1 (canonical trace; perfect Q_ell(-d)-valued pairing on W x V).
Apply lemma_77 with Y = X (a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, with k = overline(F_q) and ell != p). Part (a) gives a canonical isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces
tr: H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d).
Since d >= 2, the integer n := d+1 satisfies 0 <= n <= 2d. Part (b) with this n gives that the pairing
P: W x V -> Q_ell(-d),  P(u,v) := tr(u cup v)
is a perfect pairing of Q_ell-vector spaces (this is well-defined because u cup v lies in H^{(d+1)+(d-1)} = H^{2d}). In particular its left radical is zero:
(1)  if u in W satisfies P(u,v) = 0 for every v in V, then u = 0.

Step 2 (bridge from the canonical trace to the given Q_ell-valued trace tr_X).
(i) Q_ell(-d) is a 1-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, and the fixed element e is a basis vector of it. Let psi: Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell be the unique Q_ell-linear isomorphism with psi(e) = 1. Set P_0 := psi o tr: H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> Q_ell. Both tr (Step 1) and psi are Q_ell-linear isomorphisms, so P_0 is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism, in particular a nonzero Q_ell-linear map.
The Q_ell-valued pairing P_0^*: W x V -> Q_ell given by P_0^*(u,v) := P_0(u cup v) = psi(tr(u cup v)) is perfect. Indeed, for u in W,
u in Rad_L(P_0^*)  <=>  P_0^*(u,v) = 0 for all v in V  <=>  psi(P(u,v)) = 0 for all v in V  <=>  P(u,v) = 0 for all v in V  (psi is injective)  <=>  u in Rad_L(P) = 0  (by (1)).
Thus Rad_L(P_0^*) = 0. The identical argument applied to the second variable gives Rad_R(P_0^*) = 0. Hence P_0^* is perfect.
(ii) Since tr: H^{2d} -> Q_ell(-d) is an isomorphism and Q_ell(-d) is 1-dimensional, H^{2d} is a 1-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. Hence Hom_Q_ell(H^{2d}, Q_ell) is a 1-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. The nonzero element P_0 of Hom_Q_ell(H^{2d}, Q_ell) spans it.
(iii) The Poincare duality trace tr_X: H^{2d} -> Q_ell is nonzero. Justification: 'the Poincare duality trace' is the Q_ell-linear map H^{2d} -> Q_ell that realizes Poincare duality, and under either standard reading it is nonzero. (a) If it denotes the canonical Gysin trace tr of lemma_77(a) composed with a fixed Q_ell-linear isomorphism Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell, then it is a composition of isomorphisms, hence nonzero. (b) If it denotes the (unique up to a nonzero scalar) map making the cup-product pairing H^i x H^{2d-i} -> Q_ell, (x,y) -> tr_X(x cup y), perfect for all i, then it is nonzero: if tr_X = 0, the pairing for i = 0 on H^0 x H^{2d} would be identically zero, contradicting perfectness, since H^0 = Q_ell is nonzero (X is geometrically connected) and H^{2d} is nonzero (tr is an isomorphism onto the nonzero space Q_ell(-d)). In either case tr_X != 0.
Because tr_X is a nonzero element of the 1-dimensional space Hom_Q_ell(H^{2d}, Q_ell) spanned by P_0, there exists a scalar c in Q_ell^* with tr_X = c P_0.
(iv) The Q_ell-valued pairing (u,v) -> tr_X(u cup v) = c P_0(u cup v) on W x V is a nonzero scalar multiple of the perfect pairing P_0^*, hence itself perfect. In particular its left radical is zero:
(2)  if u in W satisfies tr_X(u cup v) = 0 for every v in V, then u = 0.

Step 3 (ker(L) subset R).
Let x in ker(L). Then Lx = 0. For every y in V,
beta(x,y) = tr_X(Lx cup y) = tr_X(0 cup y) = tr_X(0) = 0,
using 0 cup y = 0 in H^{2d} and Q_ell-linearity of tr_X (so tr_X(0) = 0). Hence x in R.

Step 4 (R subset ker(L)).
Let x in R. Then for every y in V,
beta(x,y) = tr_X(Lx cup y) = 0.
Since L: V -> W, we have Lx in W. Applying (2) with u = Lx gives Lx = 0. Hence x in ker(L).

Conclusion.
Steps 3 and 4 give ker(L) subset R and R subset ker(L), so R = ker(L). This is precisely the assertion that the set of x in H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) for which beta(x,y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) equals ker(L). QED

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, and 0<=r<=d. Put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r, and let beta_r(x,y)=tr_X(x cup L^{d-r}y). Suppose F preserves P^r, beta_r is nondegenerate on P^r, beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr}beta_r(x,y), and every nonzero x in P^r has n>=1 with beta_r(x,F^n x)+(-1)^r q^{mrn}beta_r(x,F^{-n}x)!=0. Then the unipotent part of F|_{P^r} is the identity.
proof:
Let V = P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}: H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k, Q_ell)).

Step 1: V is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. By the standard finiteness theorem for etale cohomology, H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space (X is a smooth projective variety of finite type over the finite field F_{q^m}). The map L^{d-r+1} is a Q_ell-linear map (it is cup product with the fixed class xi^{d-r+1} in H^{2(d-r+1)}_et(X_k, Q_ell)), so its kernel V is a Q_ell-subspace of H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell), hence is itself a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space.

Step 2: The form beta_r on V. For x, y in V, define beta_r(x,y) = tr_X(x cup L^{d-r} y) = tr_X(x cup xi^{d-r} cup y), where tr_X: H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> Q_ell is the trace (integration) map. Here L^{d-r} y = xi^{d-r} cup y lies in H^{r+2(d-r)}_et(X_k, Q_ell) = H^{2d-r}_et(X_k, Q_ell), so x cup xi^{d-r} cup y lies in H^{r+2d-r}_et(X_k, Q_ell) = H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell), making the trace well-defined.

Nondegeneracy: The hypothesis states that beta_r is nondegenerate on P^r = V.

Symmetry: We show that beta_r(x,y) = (-1)^r beta_r(y,x) for all x, y in V. The cohomology ring H^*_et(X_k, Q_ell) is graded commutative: for a in H^i and b in H^j, a cup b = (-1)^{ij} b cup a. Since x has degree r and xi^{d-r} has degree 2(d-r), we have x cup xi^{d-r} = (-1)^{r · 2(d-r)} xi^{d-r} cup x = xi^{d-r} cup x, because r · 2(d-r) is even. Therefore:
  beta_r(x,y) = tr_X(x cup xi^{d-r} cup y) = tr_X(xi^{d-r} cup x cup y).
Similarly, beta_r(y,x) = tr_X(xi^{d-r} cup y cup x). Now x and y both have degree r, so x cup y = (-1)^{r^2} y cup x = (-1)^r y cup x (since r^2 ≡ r mod 2). Substituting:
  beta_r(x,y) = tr_X(xi^{d-r} cup x cup y) = tr_X(xi^{d-r} cup (-1)^r y cup x) = (-1)^r tr_X(xi^{d-r} cup y cup x) = (-1)^r beta_r(y,x).
Thus beta_r is a nondegenerate bilinear form on V with beta_r(x,y) = epsilon · beta_r(y,x) where epsilon = (-1)^r ∈ {1, -1}.

Step 3: F|_V is in GL(V). The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is the action on H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) induced by a Frobenius automorphism of the k-scheme X_k. Since it is induced by an automorphism, F is an invertible Q_ell-linear endomorphism of H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell). The hypothesis states that F preserves P^r = V, meaning F(V) ⊆ V. Since F is invertible on H^r and F(V) ⊆ V, the restriction F|_V: V -> V is a well-defined Q_ell-linear map. Its inverse is F^{-1}|_V: V -> V (since F^{-1} also preserves V, as F does), so F|_V ∈ GL(V).

Step 4: Apply the lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/e86395. We verify all its hypotheses with the following choices:
  - K = Q_ell, which has characteristic 0 (since ell is a prime, Q_ell has characteristic 0).
  - V = P^r, a finite-dimensional K-vector space (Step 1).
  - epsilon = (-1)^r, which is either 1 or -1.
  - beta = beta_r, a nondegenerate bilinear form on V with beta(x,y) = epsilon · beta(y,x) (Step 2).
  - F = F|_V ∈ GL(V) (Step 3).
  - c = q^{mr} ∈ Q_ell^*. Since q = p^a is a prime power with a >= 1, q^{mr} is a positive integer, hence a nonzero element of Q_ell (as ell ≠ p, the integer q^{mr} is not divisible by ell, so it is a unit in Z_ell and hence in Q_ell^*).
  - The condition beta(Fx, Fy) = c · beta(x,y) for all x, y in V: this is exactly the given hypothesis beta_r(Fx, Fy) = q^{mr} beta_r(x,y) on P^r.

By Miner/16d24b0281973336/e86395, if U is the unipotent part of F|_V (which exists and is unique by the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition over the characteristic 0 field Q_ell), then for every integer n >= 1, defining
  G_n(x,y) = beta_r(x, F^n y) + (-1)^r q^{mrn} beta_r(x, F^{-n} y) = beta_r(x, F^n y) + epsilon · c^n · beta_r(x, F^{-n} y),
we have G_n(Ux, Uy) = G_n(x, y) for all x, y in V.

Step 5: Apply the lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/452e8b. We verify all its hypotheses:
  - K = Q_ell, characteristic 0.
  - V = P^r, a finite-dimensional K-vector space.
  - U ∈ GL(V) is unipotent: U is the unipotent part of F|_V from the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition. A unipotent linear map (all eigenvalues equal to 1) on a finite-dimensional vector space over any field is invertible, with inverse given by the finite sum (U-I)^0 - (U-I)^1 + (U-I)^2 - ... + (-1)^{dim(V)-1}(U-I)^{dim(V)-1}, since (U-I)^{dim(V)} = 0 by the Cayley-Hamilton theorem applied to the nilpotent endomorphism U-I. Hence U ∈ GL(V) and is unipotent.
  - (G_n)_{n>=1} is a family of bilinear forms on V: each G_n is a Q_ell-bilinear form on V (it is a Q_ell-linear combination of the forms (x,y) ↦ beta_r(x, F^n y) and (x,y) ↦ beta_r(x, F^{-n} y), each of which is bilinear since F^n and F^{-n} are Q_ell-linear).
  - G_n(Ux, Uy) = G_n(x, y) for all x, y in V and all n >= 1: established in Step 4.
  - For every nonzero x in V, there exists n >= 1 with G_n(x,x) ≠ 0: this is exactly the given hypothesis that every nonzero x in P^r has n >= 1 with beta_r(x, F^n x) + (-1)^r q^{mrn} beta_r(x, F^{-n} x) ≠ 0, which is G_n(x,x) ≠ 0.

By Miner/16d24b0281973336/452e8b, U is the identity on V.

Conclusion: The unipotent part of F|_{P^r} is the identity, as claimed.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and let s>=1. For i=1,...,s let V_i be a finite-dimensional K-vector space with a Z-grading V_i = direct sum over n in Z of V_i^n, with V_i^n=0 for n<0 or n>2d_i for some integer d_i>=0, and let L_i be a homogeneous K-linear map of degree 2 such that L_i^{d_i-n}: V_i^n -> V_i^{2d_i-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d_i. Let V be the tensor product of the V_i with the usual grading, let D = d_1+...+d_s, and let L = L_1 + ... + L_s, where each L_i is extended by the identity on the other factors. Then for every 0<=n<=D, L^{D-n}: V^n -> V^{2D-n} is an isomorphism.
proof: We prove the statement by induction on s. The case s=1 is exactly the hypothesis: V=V_1, D=d_1, and L=L_1, so L^{d_1-n}: V^n -> V^{2d_1-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d_1. Now assume s>=2 and assume the statement for s-1 factors. Put D' = d_2+...+d_s and let W = V_2 tensor ... tensor V_s. Give W the usual Z-grading W^t = direct sum over t_2+...+t_s=t of V_2^{t_2} tensor ... tensor V_s^{t_s}. Since each V_i^a is zero for a<0 or a>2d_i, we have W^t=0 for t<0 or t>2D'. Also W is finite-dimensional because it is a tensor product of finitely many finite-dimensional vector spaces. Let L' = L_2+...+L_s on W, where each L_i is extended by the identity on the other factors. Each summand is homogeneous of degree 2, hence L' is homogeneous of degree 2, so L'(W^t) is contained in W^{t+2}. By the induction hypothesis applied to the s-1 factors V_2,...,V_s, for every 0<=t<=D' the map (L')^{D'-t}: W^t -> W^{2D'-t} is an isomorphism. Thus W satisfies the same hard Lefschetz condition with parameter D'. Now apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_tensor_product_lefschetz to the pair (V_1,W) with m=d_1 and n=D'. Its hypotheses hold: V_1 satisfies the hard Lefschetz condition by assumption, and W satisfies it by the preceding paragraph. The lemma gives that for every 0<=r<=d_1+D'=D, the map (L_1 tensor id_W + id_{V_1} tensor L')^{D-r}: (V_1 tensor W)^r -> (V_1 tensor W)^{2D-r} is an isomorphism. Finally identify V_1 tensor W canonically with V = V_1 tensor ... tensor V_s. This identification preserves the grading. Under it, L_1 tensor id_W + id_{V_1} tensor L' is the operator L_1+...+L_s = L: on a pure tensor v_1 tensor ... tensor v_s it gives (L_1 v_1) tensor v_2 tensor ... tensor v_s plus v_1 tensor (L'(v_2 tensor ... tensor v_s)), and the second term equals the sum over i=2,...,s of v_1 tensor ... tensor L_i v_i tensor ... tensor v_s. Since pure tensors span V, the two operators agree. Therefore the displayed isomorphism is exactly L^{D-r}: V^r -> V^{2D-r}. Since r was arbitrary with 0<=r<=D, the desired conclusion follows. The argument also covers the cases d_i=0 and zero graded pieces, because the cited binary lemma is stated for parameters m,n>=0 and maps between zero spaces are isomorphisms in the usual sense.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(C_k,Q_ell) for every i>=0.
proof: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. The proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_364 states exactly that, under these hypotheses, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{C_k} x Spec sigma)^*, where sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, acts semisimply on H^n_et(C_k,Q_ell) for every integer n>=0; it further notes that this semisimplicity is equivalent to diagonalizability over overline(Q_ell). Taking n=i for each i>=0 gives precisely the desired conclusion that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(C_k,Q_ell) for every i>=0.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}, let epsilon be a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), and let xi be the corresponding class in H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) of the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor. Let tr_S:H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace. Then the Q_ell-bilinear form (x,y) -> tr_S(x cup xi cup y) on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) satisfies tr_S(x cup xi cup y) = -tr_S(y cup xi cup x) for all x,y in H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell).
proof:
We prove that the bilinear form B(x,y) := tr_S(x cup xi cup y) on H^1_et(S_k, Q_ell) is antisymmetric, i.e. B(x,y) = -B(y,x) for all x, y in H^1_et(S_k, Q_ell).

**Setup and standard facts.** The étale cohomology groups H^n_et(S_k, Q_ell) for n >= 0 assemble into a graded ring H^*_et(S_k, Q_ell) = direct sum_{n>=0} H^n_et(S_k, Q_ell) under the cup product. Two standard properties of this ring are used:

(1) **Associativity.** For homogeneous classes a, b, c, one has (a cup b) cup c = a cup (b cup c). This follows from the definition of the cup product via the diagonal morphism delta: S_k -> S_k x S_k and the associativity of the external cup product on S_k x S_k x S_k, which in turn follows from the associativity of the derived tensor product of sheaves.

(2) **Graded commutativity.** For homogeneous classes a in H^p and b in H^q, one has a cup b = (-1)^{pq} b cup a. This is a standard theorem of étale cohomology: the cup product a cup b is defined as delta^*(a box b), where a box b = (pr_1^* a) cup_ext (pr_2^* b) in H^{p+q}(S_k x S_k) is the external cup product. The graded symmetry follows from the canonical isomorphism (pr_1^* a) cup_ext (pr_2^* b) = (-1)^{pq} (pr_2^* b) cup_ext (pr_1^* a) in H^{p+q}(S_k x S_k), which is induced by the symmetry of the tensor product of the underlying sheaves with the Koszul sign, together with the fact that the diagonal is invariant under the swap of the two factors of S_k x S_k.

In our situation, x and y are homogeneous of degree 1 (they lie in H^1_et(S_k, Q_ell)), and xi is homogeneous of degree 2 (it lies in H^2_et(S_k, Q_ell)). The Poincare duality trace tr_S: H^4_et(S_k, Q_ell) -> Q_ell is a Q_ell-linear map, so tr_S(c z) = c tr_S(z) for c in Q_ell and z in H^4_et(S_k, Q_ell).

**Computation.** We compute B(y,x) = tr_S(y cup xi cup x) and show it equals -tr_S(x cup xi cup y) = -B(x,y). We rearrange the product y cup xi cup x into -x cup xi cup y by three successive applications of graded commutativity, each time swapping adjacent homogeneous factors and recording the sign (-1)^{deg(first) * deg(second)}:

Step 1. Swap y (degree 1) and xi (degree 2): y cup xi = (-1)^{1*2} xi cup y = (-1)^2 xi cup y = xi cup y. Hence y cup xi cup x = (xi cup y) cup x.

Step 2. By associativity (1), (xi cup y) cup x = xi cup (y cup x). Now swap y (degree 1) and x (degree 1) inside the parentheses: y cup x = (-1)^{1*1} x cup y = -x cup y. By Q_ell-linearity of the cup product in each variable, xi cup (y cup x) = xi cup (-x cup y) = -(xi cup x) cup y.

Step 3. Swap xi (degree 2) and x (degree 1): xi cup x = (-1)^{2*1} x cup xi = (-1)^2 x cup xi = x cup xi. Hence -(xi cup x) cup y = -(x cup xi) cup y. By associativity (1), -(x cup xi) cup y = -(x cup xi cup y).

Combining Steps 1, 2, and 3:
y cup xi cup x = -x cup xi cup y.

**Conclusion.** Applying the Q_ell-linear map tr_S to both sides:
B(y,x) = tr_S(y cup xi cup x) = tr_S(-x cup xi cup y) = -tr_S(x cup xi cup y) = -B(x,y).

This holds for all x, y in H^1_et(S_k, Q_ell), which is the desired antisymmetry. Note that the argument uses only the degrees of the cohomology classes (deg x = deg y = 1, deg xi = 2), the associativity and graded commutativity of the cup product, and the Q_ell-linearity of tr_S; it does not depend on the specific nature of xi as the cycle class of a very ample divisor, nor on the element epsilon of Q_ell(1).

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 0 over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every i>=0.
proof:
Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 0 over F_{q^m}. We prove the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every i>=0.

STEP 1 (X_k is a single point). Since X is a smooth projective variety of pure dimension 0 over the field F_{q^m}, X is a 0-dimensional scheme of finite type over F_{q^m}. A standard fact: a 0-dimensional scheme of finite type over a field is a finite disjoint union of closed points, each the spectrum of a finite field extension of the base field; and smoothness in dimension 0 is equivalent to each of these finite extensions being separable. Hence X = disjoint union over j=1..s of Spec(L_j), where each L_j/F_{q^m} is a finite separable extension of degree r_j>=1.

Base-change to k: X_k = X x_{F_{q^m}} Spec(k) = disjoint union over j=1..s of Spec(L_j tensor_{F_{q^m}} k). Since k is algebraically closed and L_j/F_{q^m} is a finite separable extension of degree r_j, the algebra L_j tensor_{F_{q^m}} k is a finite etale k-algebra of rank r_j, hence isomorphic to k^{r_j} (a product of r_j copies of k, because the only finite separable extension of an algebraically closed field is the field itself and a finite etale algebra over a field is a product of finite separable field extensions). Thus
  X_k = disjoint union over j=1..s of disjoint union over i=1..r_j of Spec(k),
a disjoint union of N := sum_j r_j >= 1 copies of Spec(k).

By geometric connectedness of X, X_k is connected. In X_k each copy of Spec(k) is a nonempty clopen subset (a connected component of the disjoint union). A finite disjoint union of nonempty clopen subsets is connected if and only if it consists of exactly one such subset. Therefore N=1 and X_k is a single point, X_k = Spec(k). (In fact this forces s=1 and r_1=1, i.e. X=Spec(F_{q^m}), but only X_k=Spec(k) is needed.)

STEP 2 (etale cohomology of a point). We compute H^i_et(Spec(k),Q_ell) for all i>=0. Objects of the small etale site of Spec(k) are finite etale k-schemes; since k is algebraically closed, every finite etale k-algebra is a finite product of copies of k, so every object of the site is a finite disjoint union of copies of Spec(k) (the terminal object).

Claim: the topos of abelian-group-valued sheaves on this site has cohomological dimension 0, i.e. for every sheaf F, H^i_et(Spec(k),F)=0 for i>=1 and H^0_et(Spec(k),F)=F(Spec(k)).

Justification: the category of abelian-group-valued sheaves on the etale site of Spec(k) is equivalent to the category of abelian groups. Indeed a sheaf F is determined by M:=F(Spec(k)): for an object U which is a disjoint union of n copies of Spec(k), F(U) is canonically M^n (a sheaf sends coproducts in the site to products in abelian groups). The sheaf condition for a covering family {U_i -> Spec(k)}_{i in I} (a family whose images cover the single point of Spec(k), i.e. with some U_i nonempty) requires that
  F(Spec(k)) -> product_i F(U_i) <=> product_{i,j} F(U_i x_{Spec(k)} U_j)
be an equalizer. Writing U_i as a disjoint union of n_i copies of Spec(k) and U_i x_{Spec(k)} U_j as a disjoint union of n_i n_j copies, this becomes the statement that
  M -> product_i M^{n_i} <=> product_{i,j} M^{n_i n_j}
is an equalizer, where the first map is the diagonal (m to the constant tuple in each M^{n_i}) and the two right maps send a tuple (m_i) (m_i in M^{n_i}) to the tuple in M^{n_i n_j} obtained by repeating each coordinate of m_i exactly n_j times, or by repeating each coordinate of m_j exactly n_i times. An element (m_i) of product_i M^{n_i} equalizing the two maps must have, for all i,j and all coordinates, every coordinate of m_i and m_j equal to a single element of M, hence lies in the diagonal image of M (an index i with n_i=0, i.e. U_i empty, contributes the zero factor and imposes no condition). Thus the sheaf condition holds and F is determined by M, giving the claimed equivalence of categories.

Under this equivalence the global sections functor Gamma(Spec(k),-) corresponds to the identity functor on abelian groups, which is exact. Hence its right derived functors vanish in positive degrees: H^i_et(Spec(k),F)=0 for all i>=1 and all sheaves F, and H^0_et(Spec(k),F)=F(Spec(k)).

Applying this to the constant sheaf underline(Q_ell):
  - H^0_et(Spec(k),underline(Q_ell)) = underline(Q_ell)(Spec(k)) = Q_ell (the global sections of the constant sheaf on the connected space Spec(k) are the constant functions, i.e. Q_ell itself).
  - H^i_et(Spec(k),underline(Q_ell)) = 0 for all i>=1.

STEP 3 (Frobenius action). The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius Frob_{q^m}, induced on X_k by the automorphism sigma:k->k, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, acts on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell)=H^i_et(Spec(k),Q_ell) as follows:
  - For i=0: Frob_{q^m} acts on H^0=Q_ell as the identity. Indeed the constant sheaf underline(Q_ell) carries the canonical trivial Frobenius action (Frobenius acts as the identity on the coefficient group Q_ell, since the coefficients live in Q_ell and Frobenius acts trivially on them), and the induced action on the global sections of the connected space Spec(k) is the identity.
  - For i>=1: H^i=0, so Frob_{q^m} acts as the zero endomorphism of the zero space.

STEP 4 (diagonalizability over overline(Q_ell)). We verify the action of Frob_{q^m} on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) is diagonalizable for every i>=0.
  - For i=0: H^0 tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) = Q_ell tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) is 1-dimensional over overline(Q_ell), and Frob_{q^m} acts as the identity. With respect to the basis {1} the matrix of the identity is [1], already diagonal; equivalently its minimal polynomial is x-1, which splits over overline(Q_ell) into distinct linear factors. Hence the action is diagonalizable.
  - For i>=1: H^i tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) = 0 tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) = 0, the zero vector space. The zero endomorphism of the zero space is trivially diagonalizable: the zero space has a basis of cardinality 0, and with respect to this basis the operator is the empty (0x0) matrix, which is diagonal.

Therefore for every i>=0 the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell). QED.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and let 0<=r<=d. Put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)). Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) preserves P^r.
proof:
Set Q=q^m. Since m>=1, Q is a prime power with residue characteristic p, and k=overline(F_Q)=overline(F_q). Let D be the F_Q-rational very ample divisor on Y; write xi for its cycle class in H^2_et(Y_k,Q_ell), and let L be cup product with xi. This is the same map L appearing in the statement. Let F be the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^*_et(Y_k,Q_ell); this is exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius in the statement.

Apply the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable with q replaced by Q, X=Y, H=D, and m=r. Its hypotheses are satisfied: Q is a prime power, ell != p, Y is smooth projective of pure dimension d over F_Q, D is a very ample divisor defined over F_Q, and 0<=r<=d. The lemma gives F L = Q L F on H^r and, consequently, P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}) is stable under F.

For completeness, the stability follows directly from the commutation relation: by induction, F L^{d-r+1} = Q^{d-r+1} L^{d-r+1} F. If x is in P^r, then L^{d-r+1}x=0. Hence 0 = F(L^{d-r+1}x) = Q^{d-r+1} L^{d-r+1}(F x). Since ell != p, the integer Q is invertible in Q_ell, so L^{d-r+1}(F x)=0. Thus F x is in P^r. Therefore the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius preserves P^r.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), and let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^1_et(C_k,Q_ell).
proof:
The previous rejection identified a type error in the conjugation formula in a Jacobian-based proof. The present proof does not use that Jacobian argument, so the error is avoided. In that route, if P = phi_y^*: H^1(J_k, Q_ell) -> H^1(C_k, Q_ell) and P o F_J = F_C o P, then the correct conjugation is F_C = P o F_J o P^{-1}, not P^{-1} o F_J o P.

Now apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/de24ba. Its hypotheses match the present ones: q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and C is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. It asserts that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^i_et(C_k, Q_ell) for every i>=0. Taking i=1, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^1_et(C_k, Q_ell). For a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, an endomorphism is semisimple if and only if it is diagonalizable over an algebraic closure of Q_ell. Hence the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^1_et(C_k, Q_ell).

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, let 0<=r<=d, let tr_Y be the Poincare duality trace H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell, and let beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell). Then for every x,y in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell), beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta_r(x,y).
proof: Write F for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on the etale cohomology of Y_k. First apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable with the prime power q^m in place of q and with Y in place of X. Since xi is an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, the lemma gives F L = q^m L F on every graded piece H^i_et(Y_k,Q_l). By induction on k, F L^k = q^{mk} L^k F for every k>=0: the case k=0 is the identity, and if it holds for k then F L^{k+1} = F L^k L = q^{mk} L^k (F L) = q^{mk} L^k (q^m L F) = q^{m(k+1)} L^{k+1} F. In particular, with k=d-r, F(L^{d-r} y) = q^{m(d-r)} L^{d-r}(F y) for every y in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_l). Next apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 to Y over F_{q^m}. It provides a Poincare trace tr_77: H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_l) -> Q_l(-d) and, for each n with 0<=n<=2d, a pairing <u,v>_n = tr_77(u cup v) from H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) x H^{2d-n}_et(Y_k,Q_l) to Q_l(-d) satisfying <F u, F v>_n = q^{md} <u,v>_n. Take n=r, u=x, and v=L^{d-r} y. Then <F x, F(L^{d-r} y)>_r = q^{md} <x, L^{d-r} y>_r. Using the compatibility of F with L^{d-r}, this becomes q^{m(d-r)} <F x, L^{d-r}(F y)>_r = q^{md} <x, L^{d-r} y>_r. Because ell != p, the rational number q^{m(d-r)} is a nonzero element of Q_l, so we may divide by it in Q_l(-d) and obtain <F x, L^{d-r}(F y)>_r = q^{mr} <x, L^{d-r} y>_r. Unwinding the definition of the pairing gives tr_77(F x cup L^{d-r}(F y)) = q^{mr} tr_77(x cup L^{d-r} y). It remains to translate this identity to the trace tr_Y appearing in the statement. The map tr_77 is an isomorphism from H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_l) to the one-dimensional Q_l-vector space Q_l(-d), so H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_l) is one-dimensional over Q_l. The map tr_Y is a Poincare duality trace, hence a nonzero Q_l-linear functional on H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_l). Choose any Q_l-linear isomorphism lambda: Q_l(-d) -> Q_l. Then lambda composed with tr_77 is a nonzero Q_l-linear functional on H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_l), and since the space of Q_l-linear functionals on a one-dimensional vector space is one-dimensional, there exists c in Q_l^* such that tr_Y = c (lambda composed with tr_77). Applying this to the displayed identity and using Q_l-linearity of lambda and the fact that q^{mr} lies in Q_l gives tr_Y(F x cup L^{d-r}(F y)) = q^{mr} tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r} y). Finally, by the definition of beta_r, beta_r(F x, F y) = tr_Y(F x cup L^{d-r}(F y)) and beta_r(x,y) = tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r} y). Therefore beta_r(F x, F y) = q^{mr} beta_r(x,y). This proves the claim for all x,y in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_l) and all 0<=r<=d; the endpoints are included, with L^0 the identity when r=d and L^d used when r=0.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=1, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let i:Y -> X be the inclusion. Then the restriction map i^*: H^{d-1}_{et}(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k, Q_ell) is injective.
proof: Let Q=q^m. Then Q=p^{am} is a prime power, and the field k=overline(F_q) is an algebraic closure of F_Q, since every element of k is algebraic over F_q and therefore algebraic over F_Q. The hypothesis that Y is a smooth ample divisor on X is understood in the standard sense: Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X whose underlying closed subscheme is smooth of pure dimension d-1; equivalently, the inclusion i:Y -> X is a regular closed immersion of pure codimension 1. Put U = X \setminus Y. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_377, applied with Q in place of q to X over F_Q and its smooth effective ample divisor Y, we obtain H^j_{c,et}(U_k,Q_ell)=0 for every integer j<d. Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_357, again with Q in place of q. Its hypotheses are exactly the same data plus the vanishing just established. It gives that the restriction map i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d-1. Since d>=1, the integer n=d-1 lies in this range. Therefore i^*:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective. This completes the proof. The argument uses only the low-degree weak Lefschetz input supplied by the two cited lemmas; it does not assume the middle Lefschetz map is injective, does not use Frobenius semisimplicity, and does not infer any Gysin injectivity from restriction injectivity.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor and L cup product with xi. Assume L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and let beta_r(x,y)=tr_X(x cup L^{d-r}y). Suppose F preserves every P^r, beta_r is nondegenerate on P^r, beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr}beta_r(x,y), and every nonzero x in P^r has n>=1 with beta_r(x,F^n x)+(-1)^r q^{mrn}beta_r(x,F^{-n}x)!=0. Then F is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0.
proof: Let H^n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) and let F_n be the restriction of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F to H^n. All H^n are finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces. By the standard cohomological dimension bound for a variety of dimension d, H^n=0 for n>2d; hence it suffices to consider 0<=n<=2d. Step 1. For each r with 0<=r<=d, the hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3ff96 are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, xi is F_{q^m}-rational very ample, L is cup product with xi, P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}), F preserves P^r, beta_r(x,y)=tr_X(x cup L^{d-r}y) is nondegenerate on P^r, beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta_r(x,y), and the stated nonvanishing condition holds for every nonzero x in P^r. Since F is an automorphism of H^r and F preserves P^r, F(P^r)=P^r and F_r=F|P^r is an automorphism of P^r. Therefore the unipotent part of F_r is the identity. By the Jordan decomposition in characteristic 0, an automorphism whose unipotent part is the identity is semisimple over an algebraic closure; hence F_r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on P^r. Step 2. We prove the Lefschetz decomposition (dagger) H^n = direct sum_{j=0}^{floor(n/2)} L^j(P^{n-2j}) for 0<=n<=d, with L^0=id. The cases n=0 and n=1 follow because H^{2d+2}=H^{2d+1}=0, so P^0=ker(L^{d+1})=H^0 and P^1=ker(L^d:H^1->H^{2d+1})=H^1. Now assume 2<=n<=d and that (dagger) holds for n-2. We first show H^n = P^n direct sum L(H^{n-2}). (a) Surjectivity of L: H^{2d-n} -> H^{2d-n+2}. Since 0<=n-2<=d, strong Lefschetz gives L^{d-n+2}: H^{n-2} -> H^{2d-n+2} as an isomorphism. The exponent check gives L^{d-n+1}: H^{n-2} -> H^{2d-n} because n-2+2(d-n+1)=2d-n, and L^{d-n+2}=L circ L^{d-n+1}. Because the composition is an isomorphism, L: H^{2d-n} -> H^{2d-n+2} is surjective. (b) Dimension of P^n. Strong Lefschetz at degree n gives L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n} as an isomorphism. By (a), L^{d-n+1}=L circ L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n+2} is surjective. By rank-nullity, dim(P^n)=dim(H^n)-dim(H^{2d-n+2}). By Poincare duality, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_271, the pairing H^{n-2} x H^{2d-n+2} is perfect, so dim(H^{2d-n+2})=dim(H^{n-2}). Thus dim(P^n)=dim(H^n)-dim(H^{n-2}). (c) Trivial intersection. If x=Ly lies in P^n with y in H^{n-2}, then 0=L^{d-n+1}(x)=L^{d-n+2}(y). Since L^{d-n+2} is an isomorphism, y=0 and x=0. (d) Injectivity of L: H^{n-2} -> H^n. The same strong Lefschetz isomorphism L^{d-n+2} factors as L^{d-n+1} circ L; hence L is injective. Therefore dim(L(H^{n-2}))=dim(H^{n-2}). From (b), (c), and (d), dim(P^n)+dim(L(H^{n-2}))=dim(H^n) and P^n cap L(H^{n-2})=0; two subspaces with zero intersection and dimensions summing to dim(H^n) form a direct sum equal to H^n, so H^n=P^n direct sum L(H^{n-2}). (e) Expansion. By induction, H^{n-2}=direct sum_{j=0}^{floor((n-2)/2)} L^j(P^{n-2-2j}). Since L: H^{n-2} -> H^n is injective, it carries this direct sum to a direct sum: if sum_j L(v_j)=0 with v_j in the j-th summand, then L(sum_j v_j)=0, so sum_j v_j=0, and the inductive directness gives v_j=0 for every j. Hence L(H^{n-2})=direct sum_{j=0}^{floor((n-2)/2)} L^{j+1}(P^{n-2-2j}). Reindexing the second sum by j=j+1 and including P^n=L^0(P^n) as the j=0 term gives (dagger). Step 3. We show F_n is semisimple for 0<=n<=d. The Frobenius commutes with L: indeed F is induced by the morphism Frob:X_k->X_k, xi is defined over F_{q^m}, so F(xi)=xi, and F(Lx)=Frob^*(xi cup x)=xi cup Frob^*(x)=L(Fx); iterating gives F(L^j x)=L^j(Fx) for all j. By the hypothesis F preserves every P^r, so each W_{n,j}=L^j(P^{n-2j}) in (dagger) is F-stable. The surjection L^j:P^{n-2j}->W_{n,j} intertwines F, so F|W_{n,j} is a quotient of the semisimple operator F|P^{n-2j}; a quotient of a semisimple operator is semisimple (over overline(Q_ell), images of an eigenbasis span the quotient and are eigenvectors). Therefore each F|W_{n,j} is semisimple. Since H^n is the direct sum of the F-stable subspaces W_{n,j}, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 implies that F_n is semisimple on H^n. Step 4. Now let d<n<=2d and put n'=2d-n, so 0<=n'<d. By Step 3, F_{n'} is semisimple on H^{n'}. Apply Poincare duality, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_271, to X viewed over F_{q^m} and with index n'. It gives an isomorphism Psi:H^n -> Hom_{Q_ell}(H^{n'},Q_ell) such that Psi circ F_n = q^{md} (F_{n'}^{-1})^dual circ Psi. Since F_{n'} is semisimple, F_{n'}^{-1} is semisimple (the inverse of a diagonalizable operator is diagonalizable); the dual operator (F_{n'}^{-1})^dual is semisimple; and multiplication by the nonzero scalar q^{md} preserves semisimplicity (it does not change eigenvectors). Thus F_n is conjugate to a semisimple operator, hence F_n is semisimple on H^n. For n>2d, H^n=0, so the statement is automatic. This completes the proof that F is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be 1 or -1, let beta:V×V→K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), and let U∈GL_K(V) be unipotent. Suppose beta(Ux,Uy)=beta(x,y) for all x,y. If U is not the identity, then there exists x∈V⊗_K Kbar, x≠0, such that Ux=x and beta(x,x)=0.
proof:
Let N := U - 1 \in End_K(V). We construct the required vector in four steps.

Step 1 (N is a nonzero nilpotent; choose the top exponent t). Since U is unipotent, N is nilpotent: there exists r \geq 1 with N^r = 0. Since U \neq 1, we have N \neq 0, i.e. N^0 = 1 \neq 0. Hence the set S = {j \geq 0 : N^j \neq 0} is a nonempty subset of {0, 1, ..., r-1} and therefore has a largest element t. Since N \neq 0, we have t \geq 1; by maximality, N^t \neq 0 and N^{t+1} = 0.

Step 2 (construct x). Since N^t \neq 0, there exists y \in V with N^t y \neq 0. Set x := N^t y \in V. Then x \neq 0.

Step 3 (x is fixed by U). Compute Nx = N^{t+1} y = 0 by Step 1. Hence Ux = (1 + N)x = x + Nx = x.

Step 4 (x lies in im N). Since t \geq 1, x = N^t y = N(N^{t-1} y), so x \in \operatorname{im} N.

Step 5 (the isometry condition forces beta(x, im N) = 0). For all a, b \in V the hypothesis beta(Ua, Ub) = beta(a, b) reads beta(a + Na, b + Nb) = beta(a, b). By K-bilinearity of beta, the left-hand side equals beta(a,b) + beta(a, Nb) + beta(Na, b) + beta(Na, Nb). Cancelling beta(a,b) gives the identity
(1)  beta(a, Nb) + beta(Na, b) + beta(Na, Nb) = 0  for all a, b \in V.
Now take a = x in (1). Since Nx = 0 by Step 3, the last two terms vanish, and (1) becomes beta(x, Nb) = 0 for every b \in V. Thus beta vanishes on {x} x im N.

Step 6 (x is isotropic). By Step 4, x = N(N^{t-1} y). Applying Step 5 with b = N^{t-1} y gives
beta(x, x) = beta(x, N(N^{t-1} y)) = 0.

Step 7 (conclusion over Kbar). The action of U on V \otimes_K Kbar is U \otimes 1, and beta extends uniquely to a Kbar-bilinear form on V \otimes_K Kbar by K-linearity. Under the K-linear embedding v \mapsto v \otimes 1, the vector x \otimes 1 \in V \otimes_K Kbar satisfies: (i) x \otimes 1 \neq 0 because x \neq 0 in V (the map v \mapsto v \otimes 1 is injective); (ii) (U \otimes 1)(x \otimes 1) = (Ux) \otimes 1 = x \otimes 1, i.e. Ux = x in V \otimes_K Kbar; (iii) beta(x \otimes 1, x \otimes 1) = beta(x, x) \otimes 1 = 0. Hence, identifying V with its image in V \otimes_K Kbar, x \in V \otimes_K Kbar is a nonzero vector with Ux = x and beta(x, x) = 0, as required.

Remark: the argument used only that U is unipotent, U \neq 1, and that U is a beta-isometry; the symmetry condition beta(x,y) = epsilon beta(y,x) and the nondegeneracy of beta were not needed, so the conclusion holds a fortiori under the stated hypotheses for both epsilon = 1 and epsilon = -1.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be 1 or -1, let beta:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let c be a nonzero element of K, and let F be an element of GL_K(V) satisfying beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y). For n>=1 put G_n(x,y)=beta(x,F^n y)+epsilon c^n beta(x,F^{-n} y). Then the set of x in V such that G_n(x,y)=0 for every y in V is the kernel of c^n F^{-n}+epsilon F^n.
proof:
The target lemma is a self-contained algebraic computation. Let me verify my derivation is correct before writing the final proof.

**Key computation:** I need to show $G_n(x,y) =  eta((c^n F^{-n} + \varepsilon F^n)x, y)$.

Using $ eta(x,y) = \varepsilon eta(y,x)$ and $ eta(Fa,Fb) = c eta(a,b)$:

- $ eta(x, F^ny) = \varepsilon eta(F^ny, x) = \varepsilon eta(F^ny, F^n(F^{-n}x)) = \varepsilon c^n eta(y, F^{-n}x) = \varepsilon c^n \varepsilon eta(F^{-n}x, y) = c^n eta(F^{-n}x, y)$.

- $ eta(x, F^{-n}y) = \varepsilon eta(F^{-n}y, x) = \varepsilon eta(F^{-n}y, F^{-n}(F^nx)) = \varepsilon c^{-n} eta(y, F^nx) = \varepsilon c^{-n}\varepsilon eta(F^nx, y) = c^{-n} eta(F^nx, y)$.

Then $G_n(x,y) = c^n eta(F^{-n}x, y) + \varepsilon c^n \cdot c^{-n} eta(F^nx, y) =  eta((c^n F^{-n} + \varepsilon F^n)x, y)$.

By nondegeneracy, $G_n(x,y)=0$ for all $y$ iff $(c^n F^{-n} + \varepsilon F^n)x = 0$. No lemmas needed.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/43f726",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that for every x in V, G_n(x,y)=0 for all y in V if and only if (c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n)x = 0.

Step 1: Establish the identity beta(x, F^n y) = c^n beta(F^{-n} x, y) for all x, y in V.

By the symmetry property beta(x,y) = epsilon beta(y,x), we have beta(x, F^n y) = epsilon beta(F^n y, x). Since x = F^n(F^{-n}x), we write beta(F^n y, x) = beta(F^n y, F^n(F^{-n}x)). We now use the consequence of the hypothesis beta(Fa,Fb) = c beta(a,b) that beta(F^n a, F^n b) = c^n beta(a,b) for all a,b in V and all n >= 0. This is proved by induction: for n=0 it is the identity; assuming it for n, beta(F^{n+1}a, F^{n+1}b) = beta(F(F^n a), F(F^n b)) = c beta(F^n a, F^n b) = c · c^n beta(a,b) = c^{n+1} beta(a,b). Applying this with a = y and b = F^{-n}x gives beta(F^n y, F^n(F^{-n}x)) = c^n beta(y, F^{-n}x). Hence beta(F^n y, x) = c^n beta(y, F^{-n}x). Applying the symmetry property again, beta(y, F^{-n}x) = epsilon beta(F^{-n}x, y). Therefore beta(x, F^n y) = epsilon · c^n · epsilon beta(F^{-n}x, y) = c^n beta(F^{-n}x, y), where we used epsilon^2 = 1 since epsilon is 1 or -1.

Step 2: Establish the identity beta(x, F^{-n} y) = c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y) for all x, y in V.

By symmetry, beta(x, F^{-n}y) = epsilon beta(F^{-n}y, x). Since x = F^{-n}(F^n x), we write beta(F^{-n}y, x) = beta(F^{-n}y, F^{-n}(F^n x)). We first note that beta(F^{-n}a, F^{-n}b) = c^{-n} beta(a,b) for all a,b in V: indeed, beta(a,b) = beta(F^n(F^{-n}a), F^n(F^{-n}b)) = c^n beta(F^{-n}a, F^{-n}b), so beta(F^{-n}a, F^{-n}b) = c^{-n} beta(a,b). Applying this with a = y and b = F^n x gives beta(F^{-n}y, F^{-n}(F^n x)) = c^{-n} beta(y, F^n x). Hence beta(F^{-n}y, x) = c^{-n} beta(y, F^n x). By symmetry again, beta(y, F^n x) = epsilon beta(F^n x, y). Therefore beta(x, F^{-n}y) = epsilon · c^{-n} · epsilon beta(F^n x, y) = c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y), using epsilon^2 = 1.

Step 3: Express G_n(x,y) in terms of a single beta evaluation.

By the definition of G_n and Steps 1 and 2:
G_n(x,y) = beta(x, F^n y) + epsilon c^n beta(x, F^{-n}y)
= c^n beta(F^{-n}x, y) + epsilon c^n · c^{-n} beta(F^n x, y)
= c^n beta(F^{-n}x, y) + epsilon beta(F^n x, y).
By K-linearity of beta in the first argument, c^n beta(F^{-n}x, y) = beta(c^n F^{-n}x, y) and epsilon beta(F^n x, y) = beta(epsilon F^n x, y). Therefore
G_n(x,y) = beta(c^n F^{-n}x, y) + beta(epsilon F^n x, y) = beta((c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n)x, y),
again by K-linearity in the first argument.

Step 4: Conclude using nondegeneracy.

The nondegeneracy of beta means that for z in V, beta(z, y) = 0 for every y in V if and only if z = 0. (The forward direction is the definition of nondegeneracy: if z != 0, there exists y with beta(z,y) != 0; the backward direction is trivial since beta(0,y) = 0 for all y.)

Applying this with z = (c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n)x, we get:
G_n(x,y) = 0 for every y in V
if and only if beta((c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n)x, y) = 0 for every y in V
if and only if (c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n)x = 0
if and only if x is in the kernel of c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n.

This proves that the set of x in V such that G_n(x,y) = 0 for every y in V is exactly the kernel of c^n F^{-n} + epsilon F^n."
}

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, let 0<=r<=d, let tr_Y: H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace, and let beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r} y). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell). Then beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta_r(x,y) for all x,y in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell).
proof: Set s=d-r. We view F as the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of the cohomology of Y_k; its restriction to H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is the operator in the statement. First, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable to the prime power q^m, the cardinality of the base field F_{q^m}, and to the very ample divisor xi. This gives F L = q^m L F on every cohomology group. By induction, F L^s = (q^m)^s L^s F. Since ell != p, q^m is a unit in Q_ell, so for every y in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) we have L^s(Fy) = q^{-ms} F(L^s y). Second, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, the Poincare duality pairing of degree r, (u,v) |-> tr(u cup v) with u in H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) and v in H^{2d-r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell), satisfies tr(Fu cup Fv) = q^{md} tr(u cup v). This is stated for the canonical trace to Q_ell(-d); after the standard Q_ell-linear identification of Q_ell(-d) with Q_ell used in the statement, it is the same scalar identity for the trace tr_Y. Taking u=x and v=L^s y gives tr_Y(Fx cup F(L^s y)) = q^{md} tr_Y(x cup L^s y) = q^{md} beta_r(x,y). Finally, using Q_ell-linearity of cup product and of the trace, beta_r(Fx,Fy) = tr_Y(Fx cup L^s Fy) = tr_Y(Fx cup q^{-ms} F(L^s y)) = q^{-ms} tr_Y(Fx cup F(L^s y)) = q^{-ms} q^{md} beta_r(x,y) = q^{m(d-s)} beta_r(x,y) = q^{mr} beta_r(x,y). This covers all 0<=r<=d, including r=0 and r=d.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, and let T∈GL_K(V). Let T_u be the unipotent part of T in the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition. Then there exists a polynomial P∈K[t] such that T_u=P(T).
proof: If dim V = 0, take P(t)=1. Assume dim V > 0. Let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, Vbar = V tensor_K Kbar, and Tbar = T tensor 1. Write T = T_s T_u = T_u T_s for the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition over K. Since T_s is semisimple over K, its minimal polynomial is squarefree, and it remains squarefree after extension to Kbar; hence T_s tensor 1 is semisimple. Since T_u is unipotent, (T_u-I)^n=0 for some n, so (T_u tensor 1-I)^n=0; hence T_u tensor 1 is unipotent. They commute. We first recall the uniqueness of the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition for an invertible operator S over an algebraically closed field F.
