If S = A B = B A with A semisimple and B unipotent, then A and B preserve every generalized eigenspace W_lambda of S. On W_lambda, S = lambda(I+N) with N nilpotent, and lambda is nonzero. Since B is unipotent, the inverse of B is unipotent; since B commutes with S, the inverse of B commutes with N. Hence A|W_lambda = S|W_lambda (inverse of B)|W_lambda = lambda(I+N)(inverse of B) is lambda times a product of commuting unipotent operators, so it is lambda times a unipotent operator. But A is semisimple; an operator of the form lambda U with U unipotent has only the eigenvalue lambda, and if it is semisimple it must be lambda I. Thus A|W_lambda = lambda I and B|W_lambda = (1/lambda) S|W_lambda = I+N. This proves uniqueness, and in particular T_u tensor 1 is the unipotent part of Tbar. Now let m(t) be the minimal polynomial of T over K. Because T is invertible, m(0) != 0. Over Kbar, m(t) = product_j (t - lambda_j)^{e_j}, where lambda_1,...,lambda_s are the distinct eigenvalues of Tbar (all nonzero) and e_j is the nilpotency index of Tbar - lambda_j I on the generalized lambda_j-eigenspace W_j = ker(Tbar - lambda_j I)^{e_j}. The W_j form a direct sum decomposition of Vbar. On W_j put N_j = (Tbar - lambda_j I)/lambda_j; then N_j^{e_j}=0 and Tbar|W_j = lambda_j(I+N_j). By the uniqueness just described, the unipotent part Tbar_u of Tbar restricts to I+N_j on W_j, i.e. Tbar_u|W_j = Tbar/lambda_j|W_j. We now construct a polynomial. The moduli (t - lambda_j)^{e_j} in Kbar[t] are pairwise coprime. By the Chinese remainder theorem there is a unique class of Q in Kbar[t] modulo M(t) = product_j (t - lambda_j)^{e_j} = m(t) such that Q(t) - t/lambda_j is divisible by (t - lambda_j)^{e_j} for every j. Choose the representative Q with degree less than deg m. We claim Q has coefficients in K. Let sigma be an element of the Galois group Gal(Kbar/K). Because m(t) is in K[t], sigma permutes the lambda_j and preserves the exponents e_j. Applying sigma to the congruences shows that sigma(Q) satisfies the same system of congruences. By uniqueness modulo m, sigma(Q) is congruent to Q modulo m. Since deg sigma(Q) <= deg Q < deg m, we get sigma(Q) = Q. Thus Q is fixed by all sigma, and the fixed field of Gal(Kbar/K) is K, so Q is in K[t]. Put P = Q. For each j there is R_j in Kbar[t] with P(t) - t/lambda_j = (t - lambda_j)^{e_j} R_j(t). Evaluating at Tbar gives P(Tbar) - Tbar/lambda_j = (Tbar - lambda_j I)^{e_j} R_j(Tbar). Restricting to W_j, the right hand side is zero, so P(Tbar)|W_j = Tbar/lambda_j|W_j = Tbar_u|W_j. Since Vbar is the direct sum of the W_j, P(Tbar) = Tbar_u. But P(Tbar) = P(T) tensor 1 and Tbar_u = T_u tensor 1, so P(T) tensor 1 = T_u tensor 1. The natural map End_K(V) to End_Kbar(Vbar) is injective, hence P(T) = T_u. This proves the existence of P in K[t].

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, let tr_Y:H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace, and let beta_0(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^d y) for x,y in H^0_et(Y_k,Q_ell). Then beta_0 is nondegenerate.
proof: Set Q = q^m. Then Q is a prime power and k = overline(F_q) = overline(F_Q). The variety Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 2 over F_Q, and xi is the cycle class of an F_Q-rational very ample divisor under the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_358_top_degree, cup product with xi^d, i.e. L^d, is an isomorphism H^0_et(Y_k,Q_ell) -> H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell). We record that H^0_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is one-dimensional with basis 1. Indeed Y_k is geometrically connected, hence connected. A global section of the constant sheaf Q_ell on the etale site is an etale-locally constant Q_ell-valued function; since etale morphisms are open, such a function is locally constant on the underlying topological space, and since Y_k is connected it is constant. Thus the constant functions give all sections, and the constant function 1 is a nonzero generator. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, the Poincare duality trace gives a canonical isomorphism H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d); under the identifications of Tate twists with Q_ell appearing in the statement, this is the map tr_Y, so tr_Y is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism. Let 1 denote the generator of H^0. Since L^d is an isomorphism and 1 != 0, z := L^d(1) is a nonzero element of H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell). Since tr_Y is an isomorphism, c := tr_Y(z) is a nonzero element of Q_ell. Now take arbitrary x,y in H^0. Write x = a 1 and y = b 1 with a,b in Q_ell. By linearity of L, L^d y = b L^d 1 = b z. Since 1 is the unit for cup product, x cup L^d y = (a 1) cup (b z) = ab (1 cup z) = ab z. Hence beta_0(x,y) = tr_Y(x cup L^d y) = tr_Y(ab z) = ab c. Thus beta_0 is the nonzero scalar c times the product of the Q_ell-coordinates of x and y. If beta_0(x,y)=0 for every y, then taking y=1 gives beta_0(x,1)=a c=0, so a=0 and x=0. If beta_0(x,y)=0 for every x, then taking x=1 gives beta_0(1,y)=b c=0, so b=0 and y=0. Therefore both radicals of beta_0 are zero, so beta_0 is nondegenerate.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, let 0<=r<=d, put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) preserving P^r, and let beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y). Suppose beta_r(x,y)=(-1)^r beta_r(y,x), beta_r restricted to P^r is nondegenerate, and beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr}beta_r(x,y). Let U be the unipotent part of F|_{P^r}. If U is not the identity, then there exists x in P^r⊗_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell), x≠0, such that Ux=x and beta_r(x,x)=0.
proof: Put K=Q_ell and V=P^r. The etale cohomology group H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over K by the standard finiteness theorem for smooth projective varieties over finite fields; hence V is a finite-dimensional K-vector space. If V=0, then U=id_V, contrary to the hypothesis that U is not the identity; thus in the present case V is nonzero. Let beta be the restriction of beta_r to V x V. By hypothesis beta is nondegenerate (hence perfect, since V is finite-dimensional), and beta(x,y)=(-1)^r beta(y,x) for all x,y in V; set epsilon=(-1)^r. Since ell != p, q^{mr} is a nonzero element of K. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is the pullback by the automorphism x -> x^{q^m} of Y_k; its inverse is the pullback by the inverse automorphism. Therefore it is invertible on every etale cohomology group, and its restriction to the F-stable subspace V is an element of GL_K(V). Because F preserves V, for x,y in V we have Fx,Fy in V and the hypothesis beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta_r(x,y) gives beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta(x,y). Apply the proved lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/bc7724 to K, V, the perfect bilinear form beta, c=q^{mr}, and T=F|_V. It yields that the unipotent part U of T in the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition satisfies beta(Ux,Uy)=beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. By definition this U is the unipotent part of F|_{P^r} in the target statement. Now apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/430204 with K=Q_ell, Kbar=overline(Q_ell), V=P^r, epsilon=(-1)^r, beta as above, and U. Its hypotheses are satisfied: V is finite-dimensional, beta is nondegenerate and epsilon-symmetric, U is unipotent and invertible, and U is a beta-isometry. Since U is assumed not the identity, the lemma gives a nonzero x in V tensor_K Kbar = P^r tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) such that Ux=x and beta(x,x)=0. The last equality is beta_r(x,x)=0 because beta is the restriction of beta_r and the latter extends bilinearly to the scalar extension. This proves the claim. The previous invalid adjoint step is avoided: no identity beta(Uz,U inverse w)=beta(z,w) is asserted; the required isotropic fixed vector follows directly from Miner/16d24b0281973336/430204 after the isometry property is established by Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/bc7724.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be 1 or -1, let beta:V×V→K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F∈GL_K(V), and let c∈K^×. Suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y. Let U be the unipotent part of F. If U is not the identity, then there exists x∈V⊗_K Kbar, x≠0, such that for every n≥1, beta(x,F^n x)+epsilon c^n beta(x,F^{-n}x)=0.
proof: We prove the statement after scalar extension to Kbar, still writing V and beta. The form remains nondegenerate and the hypotheses are unchanged. The unipotent part remains nontrivial after this extension: in the rational canonical form over K, the exponents of the elementary divisors are the sizes of the corresponding Jordan blocks after splitting the irreducible factors over Kbar, and characteristic 0 makes this splitting separable. Thus if F were semisimple over Kbar, all those exponents would be 1, so F would be semisimple over K, contradicting U != I. Therefore F is not semisimple over Kbar. Let d=dim V. For lambda in Kbar^* set V_lambda=ker(F-lambda I)^d. Since Kbar is algebraically closed, V is the direct sum of the V_lambda, and each V_lambda is stable under F and F^{-1}. For A in End(V) let A^* be the adjoint defined by beta(Ax,y)=beta(x,A^*y). For all x,y, beta(Fx,Fy)=beta(x,F^*F y) by the definition of F^*, while the hypothesis gives beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y); nondegeneracy gives F^*F=cI, hence F^*=cF^{-1}. Claim: if x in V_lambda, y in V_mu, and lambda mu != c, then beta(x,y)=0. Indeed, for y in V_mu we have (F-mu I)^d y=0. Since (F-mu I)F^{-1}=-mu(F^{-1}-mu^{-1}I) and F commutes with F^{-1}, this implies (F^{-1}-mu^{-1}I)^d y=0. Using F^*=cF^{-1}, we get (F^*-c/mu I)^d y=0; hence F^* preserves V_mu and F^*|V_mu=(c/mu)I plus a nilpotent. If lambda mu != c, then lambda != c/mu, so F^*-lambda I is invertible on V_mu. For any z in V_mu put w=(F^*-lambda I)^{-d}z. Then beta(x,z)=beta(x,(F^*-lambda I)^d w)=beta((F-lambda I)^d x,w)=0, because x in V_lambda. This proves the claim. Since F is not semisimple over Kbar, for at least one lambda the nilpotent operator N_lambda=lambda^{-1}F|V_lambda-I is nonzero. Case 1: lambda^2 != c. Choose 0 != x in V_lambda. For every n>=1, F^n x and F^{-n}x lie in V_lambda. Applying the claim with mu=lambda gives beta(x,F^n x)=0 and beta(x,F^{-n}x)=0, so the required expression is 0. Case 2: lambda^2=c. Put W=V_lambda. The restriction of beta to W is nondegenerate: if x in W is orthogonal to W, then the claim shows it is orthogonal to every V_mu with mu != lambda, and because lambda^2=c the only remaining generalized eigenspace is V_lambda itself, so x is orthogonal to V and hence x=0. Let T=lambda^{-1}F|W. Then T=I+N_lambda is unipotent and T != I. Also beta(Tx,Ty)=lambda^{-2}beta(Fx,Fy)=lambda^{-2}c beta(x,y)=beta(x,y), so T is an isometry of the nondegenerate epsilon-symmetric form beta|W. On W, write A^* for the adjoint with respect to beta|W. We now prove that such a T admits 0 != x in W with T^n x=x for all n>=1 and beta(x,x)=0. Let m=dim W and set Y=log T=sum from j=1 to m of (-1)^{j+1}(T-I)^j/j. Since T-I is nilpotent, the sum is finite, Y is nilpotent, and the formal identities T=exp(Y) and T^{-1}=exp(-Y) hold in characteristic 0 because the series terminate and the usual formal power-series identities apply. Because T is an isometry, T^*T=I, so T^*=T^{-1}. Since Y is a polynomial in T-I, Y^* is the same polynomial in T^*-I, namely Y^*=log(T^{-1}). The formal identity log(exp(Z))=Z for nilpotent Z gives log(T^{-1})=log(exp(-Y))=-Y, so Y^*=-Y. Since T != I, Y != 0. A nonzero nilpotent operator has ker Y intersect im Y nonzero: if the intersection were zero, the restriction of Y to im Y would be injective; since im Y^k is contained in im Y for k>=1, the same injectivity would give rank(Y^{k+1})=rank(Y^k) for all k>=1, hence rank(Y^m)=rank(Y), contradicting Y^m=0 and Y !=0. Choose 0 != x in ker Y intersect im Y. For y in ker Y and any z, 0=beta(Y y,z)=beta(y,Y^* z)=-beta(y,Y z), so every y in ker Y is orthogonal to im Y. In particular beta(x,x)=0. Also T^n x=exp(nY)x=x and T^{-n}x=exp(-nY)x=x for all n>=1. Thus beta(x,T^n x)+epsilon beta(x,T^{-n}x)=beta(x,x)+epsilon beta(x,x)=0. Returning to F, for this x in W we have F^n x=lambda^n T^n x=lambda^n x and F^{-n}x=lambda^{-n}x. Since c=lambda^2, the target expression equals lambda^n beta(x,x)+epsilon c^n lambda^{-n} beta(x,x)=lambda^n(1+epsilon)beta(x,x)=0. The vector x is nonzero and lies in V tensor Kbar, as required. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let beta:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form, let F be in GL_K(V), and let c be a nonzero element of K. Suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Let U be the unipotent part of F in the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition. Then beta(Ux,Uy)=beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.
proof: Let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K. We first prove the assertion after extending scalars to Kbar. The Jordan-Chevalley decomposition is compatible with field extension: if F = S U = U S over K with S semisimple and U unipotent, then over Kbar the same S and U give the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition, because U is still unipotent, S is still semisimple (its minimal polynomial remains square-free and splits into distinct linear factors), and the decomposition is unique in characteristic 0. Thus we may assume K is algebraically closed. Let S be the semisimple part, so F = S U = U S. Since F is invertible and U is unipotent, U is invertible, so S = F U⁻¹ is invertible. Let Lambda be the set of eigenvalues of S. Because S is semisimple, V is the direct sum of the eigenspaces V_lambda = ker(S - lambda I) for lambda in Lambda. The operators S and U commute, so U preserves each V_lambda. Put U_lambda = U|_{V_lambda}; then U_lambda = I + N_lambda with N_lambda nilpotent. For n >= 1, F^n is a similitude with multiplier c^n: this is immediate for n = 1, and if beta(F^n x, F^n y) = c^n beta(x,y), then beta(F^{n+1} x, F^{n+1} y) = beta(F(F^n x), F(F^n y)) = c beta(F^n x, F^n y) = c^{n+1} beta(x,y). Fix lambda, mu in Lambda and set d = c / (lambda mu). The eigenvalues are nonzero because S is invertible. For x in V_lambda and y in V_mu, we have F^n x = lambda^n U_lambda^n x and F^n y = mu^n U_mu^n y. Applying the similitude identity to F^n x and F^n y gives lambda^n mu^n beta(U_lambda^n x, U_mu^n y) = c^n beta(x,y), hence beta(U_lambda^n x, U_mu^n y) = d^n beta(x,y). If beta is identically zero on V_lambda x V_mu, then taking n = 1 in this identity gives beta(U x, U y) = 0 = beta(x,y) for all such x and y. Otherwise choose x0, y0 with beta(x0, y0) != 0. Choose integers r and s such that N_lambda^(r+1) = 0 and N_mu^(s+1) = 0. For every positive integer n, U_lambda^n = (I + N_lambda)^n = sum_{j=0}^r binom(n,j) N_lambda^j and U_mu^n = (I + N_mu)^n = sum_{k=0}^s binom(n,k) N_mu^k, where binom(n,j) is the value at n of the polynomial t(t-1)...(t-j+1)/j!. Therefore the function n -> beta(U_lambda^n x0, U_mu^n y0) / beta(x0, y0) is a polynomial P(n) over Kbar. The identity above says P(n) = d^n for every n >= 1. We claim d = 1. Suppose d != 1. Let m = deg P. The (m+1)-st forward difference of a polynomial of degree m is identically zero. On the other hand, since P(n) = d^n for all n >= 1, the (m+1)-st forward difference of P at n equals the (m+1)-st forward difference of the sequence n -> d^n, namely (d - 1)^(m+1) * d^n. This last expression is nonzero because d is nonzero and d != 1. This contradiction forces d = 1. With d = 1, the identity with n = 1 gives beta(U_lambda x, U_mu y) = beta(x,y) for all x in V_lambda and y in V_mu. Together with the zero case, this proves the desired equality on every pair of S-eigenspaces. Now let x and y be arbitrary elements of V. Write x = sum_lambda x_lambda and y = sum_mu y_mu with x_lambda in V_lambda and y_mu in V_mu. Since U preserves each V_lambda and beta is bilinear, beta(U x, U y) = sum_{lambda,mu} beta(U_lambda x_lambda, U_mu y_mu) = sum_{lambda,mu} beta(x_lambda, y_mu) = beta(x,y). Thus the identity holds over Kbar. Restricting to the original K-vector space V gives beta(U x, U y) = beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, let 0<=r<=d, put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell), and let tr_Y be the Poincare duality trace H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell. Let beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y) for x,y in P^r. Suppose F preserves P^r, beta_r restricted to P^r is nondegenerate, and beta_r(Fx,Fy)=q^{mr} beta_r(x,y) for all x,y in P^r. Then the multiset of eigenvalues of F|_{P^r} over overline(Q_ell) is invariant under the map lambda -> q^{mr}/lambda.
proof: Let V = P^r and let T = F|_V. Write beta for the restriction of beta_r to V x V, and put c = q^{mr}. Since ell != p, the integer q is nonzero in Q_ell, hence c is a nonzero element of Q_ell. The Frobenius action on l-adic cohomology with Q_ell coefficients is Q_ell-linear, so T is a Q_ell-linear endomorphism of V. The group H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell by the standard finiteness theorem for l-adic cohomology of smooth projective varieties, so V is finite-dimensional. If V = 0, the multiset of eigenvalues is empty and the assertion is trivial; hence assume V != 0. We first show that T is invertible. If x in ker(T), then for every y in V we have 0 = beta(Tx,Ty) = c beta(x,y). Since c != 0, beta(x,y) = 0 for all y in V. Nondegeneracy of beta on V gives x = 0. Thus T is injective, and finite-dimensionality of V implies T is an automorphism of V. Because beta is nondegenerate on the finite-dimensional space V, it is a perfect pairing. Let T^dagger be the adjoint of T with respect to beta, defined by beta(Tx,y) = beta(x,T^dagger y). For all x,y in V, the hypothesis gives beta(Tx,Ty) = c beta(x,y), while the definition of the adjoint gives beta(Tx,Ty) = beta(x,T^dagger T y). Hence beta(x,(T^dagger T - c id_V)y) = 0 for all x,y in V. Nondegeneracy implies T^dagger T = c id_V. Since T is invertible, T^dagger = c T^{-1}. Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_69 to k = Q_ell, this finite-dimensional nonzero V, T, c, and the perfect pairing beta. Part (3) of that lemma says that the multiset of eigenvalues of T over overline(Q_ell), counted with algebraic multiplicity, coincides with the multiset obtained by replacing each eigenvalue lambda by c/lambda. This is exactly the desired invariance for F|_{P^r} with c = q^{mr}.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be 1 or -1, let beta:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let c be a nonzero element of K, let F be an element of GL_K(V) satisfying beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y), and for n>=1 put G_n(x,y)=beta(x,F^n y)+epsilon c^n beta(x,F^{-n} y). If for every nonzero x in V there exists n>=1 with G_n(x,x)!=0, then the bilinear form (a,b)->Tr_V(a b^dag) on K[F] is nondegenerate, where b^dag is the adjoint of b with respect to beta.
proof: Let A=K[F]. If V=0, then A is the zero vector space and the assertion is vacuous, so assume V is nonzero. Write F=F_s F_u=F_u F_s for the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition over K, with F_s semisimple and F_u unipotent. By the cited lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/bc7724, the unipotent part F_u is an isometry for beta, i.e. beta(F_u x,F_u y)=beta(x,y) for all x,y. Suppose F_u is not the identity. Put N=F_u-1. Then N is a nonzero nilpotent endomorphism. Expanding the isometry identity gives beta(Nx,y)+beta(x,Ny)+beta(Nx,Ny)=0 for all x,y. If y is in ker N, this becomes beta(Nx,y)=0 for all x, so im N is orthogonal to ker N. Since beta(u,v)=epsilon beta(v,u), ker N is orthogonal to im N as well. Because N is a nonzero nilpotent, choose x with N^r x nonzero and N^{r+1} x=0 for some r>=1; then z=N^r x is nonzero, lies in im N, and satisfies Nz=0, so W=ker N cap im N is nonzero. If u and v are in W, then u is in ker N and v is in im N, hence beta(u,v)=0; thus W is totally isotropic. Since F_s commutes with F_u, it commutes with N. Therefore F_s(ker N)=ker N and F_s(im N)=im N, so F_s(W)=W. For any x in W, F_u x=x and F_u^{-1}x=x, hence F^n x=F_s^n x and F^{-n}x=F_s^{-n}x for every n>=1, and both vectors lie in W. Because W is totally isotropic, beta(x,F^n x)=0 and beta(x,F^{-n}x)=0 for every n>=1. Consequently G_n(x,x)=beta(x,F^n x)+epsilon c^n beta(x,F^{-n}x)=0 for every n>=1, contradicting the hypothesis applied to the nonzero vector x. Hence F_u=1, and F is semisimple. Next we prove that B(a,b)=Tr_V(a b^dag) is nondegenerate on A. The adjoint map dagger is an anti-automorphism of End_K(V), since beta((ab)x,y)=beta(bx,a^dag y)=beta(x,b^dag a^dag y). It is an involution because beta is epsilon-symmetric: in a basis with matrix M for beta, M^T=epsilon M, the matrix of b^dag is M^{-1} b^T M, and applying the same formula twice returns b. From beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) we get beta(Fx,y)=c beta(x,F^{-1}y) for all x,y, so F^dag=c F^{-1}. Since F is invertible, F^{-1} is a polynomial in F by Cayley-Hamilton, hence F^dag lies in A. Because dagger is an anti-automorphism and fixes K, it maps A into A; since it is an involution, its restriction to A is a bijection of A onto itself. Define T(a,d)=Tr_V(a d). If a is orthogonal to every b with respect to B, then Tr_V(a b^dag)=0 for all b in A. As b^dag ranges over all of A, this says Tr_V(a d)=0 for all d in A, so a is in the radical of T. The reverse inclusion is immediate, so the radicals of B and T coincide. It remains to show T is nondegenerate. Since F is semisimple, its minimal polynomial mu_F is squarefree. The natural map K[t] to A has kernel (mu_F), so A is isomorphic to K[t]/(mu_F). Write mu_F as a product of distinct irreducible polynomials f_i. By the Chinese remainder theorem, A is isomorphic to the product of the finite field extensions L_i=K[t]/(f_i). Let e_i be the corresponding idempotents in A and put V_i=e_i V. Then V is the direct sum of the V_i. For each i with V_i nonzero, V_i is a nonzero finite-dimensional L_i-vector space; set m_i=dim_{L_i} V_i. For a=(a_i) and d=(d_i) in A, the operator ad acts on V_i as multiplication by a_i d_i, so Tr_V(ad)=sum_i m_i Tr_{L_i/K}(a_i d_i), with terms for V_i=0 omitted. Fix a nonzero a and choose i with a_i nonzero. The trace pairing on L_i is nondegenerate: L_i/K is finite separable because char K=0; after extending scalars to an algebraic closure, L_i tensor Kbar is a product of copies of Kbar, and the extended trace pairing is (u,v) to sum_j u_j v_j, which is nondegenerate; if the original pairing had a nonzero radical r, then r tensor 1 would be a nonzero radical after scalar extension. Hence there exists d_i in L_i with Tr_{L_i/K}(a_i d_i) nonzero. Choose d in A whose i-th component is d_i and whose other components are 0. Then T(a,d)=m_i Tr_{L_i/K}(a_i d_i) is nonzero. Thus no nonzero a is orthogonal to all d, so T is nondegenerate. Since the radicals of B and T coincide, B is nondegenerate.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, and let L be cup product with xi. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d-2, and suppose L:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is injective. Then L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d.
proof: Let Q=q^m. Then Q is a prime power, and X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_Q. We identify the algebraic closure of F_Q with the given k. The given F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor is an F_Q-rational very ample divisor, and L is cup product with its cycle class. Apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_333 to the prime power Q, this variety X, this divisor, and this L. It asserts that for every integer n with 0<=n<=d, the Q_ell-linear map L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is injective if and only if it is surjective. For n=d-1, this map is exactly L:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell). By the hypothesis, this map is injective; hence by the cited lemma it is surjective. Since it is both injective and surjective, it is an isomorphism. For n=d, L^0 is the identity map on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), hence an isomorphism. For 0<=n<=d-2, the required isomorphism is precisely the hypothesis. Therefore L^{d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m} that is geometrically connected, and let i:Y->X be the inclusion. Suppose the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) for every integer r with 0<=r<d. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every integer r with 0<=r<d.
proof:
Let U = X \setminus Y denote the open complement of Y in X, with open immersion j:U\hookrightarrow X and closed immersion i:Y\hookrightarrow X. Let F_X and F_Y denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms on the respective étale cohomology groups.

**Step 1: Vanishing of compactly supported cohomology of U.**
Since X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d \geq 1 over F_{q^m} (where q^m = p^{am} is a prime power with the same underlying prime p), and Y \subset X is an effective ample divisor defined over F_{q^m} that is smooth of pure dimension d-1, we may apply the vanishing result [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_377] with the prime power q^m in place of q. This yields:
\[ H^j_{c,\acute{e}t}(U_k, \mathbb{Q}_\ell) = 0 \quad \text{for every integer } j < d. \]

**Step 2: The localization sequence and Frobenius equivariance.**
By the localization long exact sequence [Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283], applied with the prime power q^m, there is a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector spaces
\[ \cdots \to H^r_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^r_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^{r+1}_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to \cdots \]
whose middle map is the pullback i^*, and in which every map commutes with the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of the four terms. In particular, i^* \circ F_X = F_Y \circ i^* at the relevant degrees.

**Step 3: The case 0 \leq r \leq d-2 (isomorphism).**
Fix r with 0 \leq r \leq d-2. Then r < d and r+1 \leq d-1 < d. By Step 1:
\[ H^r_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad H^{r+1}_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = 0. \]
From the exact sequence in Step 2, the segment
\[ 0 \to H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^r_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to 0 \]
is exact, so i^*: H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^r_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) is an isomorphism of \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector spaces.

Since i^* commutes with Frobenius (Step 2), we have i^* \circ F_X|_{H^r(X)} = F_Y|_{H^r(Y)} \circ i^*. As i^* is an isomorphism, it follows that
\[ F_X|_{H^r(X)} = (i^*)^{-1} \circ F_Y|_{H^r(Y)} \circ i^*, \]
so F_X|_{H^r(X)} is conjugate (similar) to F_Y|_{H^r(Y)}.

By hypothesis, F_Y is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^r_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) for every r with 0 \leq r < d; in particular this holds for the current r \leq d-2 < d. Diagonalizability over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell is preserved under similarity: if F_Y \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalizable on H^r(Y)\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell, then so is (i^*)^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id} \circ (F_Y\otimes\mathrm{id}) \circ (i^*\otimes\mathrm{id}) = F_X\otimes\mathrm{id} on H^r(X)\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell. Hence F_X is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).

**Step 4: The case r = d-1 (injectivity and restriction to a stable subspace).**
Now take r = d-1. Since d \geq 2, we have d-1 \geq 1, and in any case d-1 < d. By Step 1:
\[ H^{d-1}_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = 0. \]
From the exact sequence in Step 2, the segment
\[ 0 \to H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^d_c(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to \cdots \]
shows that i^*: H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \hookrightarrow H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) is injective.

Let W := \operatorname{im}(i^*) \subseteq H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell). Since i^* \circ F_X = F_Y \circ i^*, for any x \in H^{d-1}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) we have F_Y(i^*(x)) = i^*(F_X(x)) \in W, so W is F_Y-stable.

The map i^* identifies H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) with W as \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector spaces, and under this identification the operator F_X|_{H^{d-1}(X)} corresponds to the restriction F_Y|_W. By hypothesis, F_Y is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) (since d-1 < d). An operator that is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell is semisimple in the sense that its minimal polynomial over \mathbb{Q}_\ell is a product of distinct irreducible polynomials. By the restriction lemma [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515], the restriction of a semisimple \mathbb{Q}_\ell-linear operator to a stable subspace is again semisimple. Therefore F_Y|_W is semisimple, i.e., diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell. Consequently, F_X is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).

**Step 5: Conclusion.**
For every integer r with 0 \leq r < d, we have two cases:
- If 0 \leq r \leq d-2, Step 3 shows that F_X is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).
- If r = d-1, Step 4 shows that F_X is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^{d-1}_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).

Since d \geq 2, the range 0 \leq r < d is the disjoint union of \{0, 1, \ldots, d-2\} and \{d-1\}, so every r with 0 \leq r < d is covered. This completes the proof that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell on H^r_{\acute{e}t}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) for every integer r with 0 \leq r < d. \blacksquare

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell).
proof: Write Q_ellbar for an algebraic closure of Q_ell. Let F_m denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V = H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell). We prove F_m is diagonalizable over Q_ellbar. First choose a smooth ample curve after a finite extension. Since X is projective over F_{q^m}, there is a closed immersion X -> P^s_{F_{q^m}}; the pullback L of O_{P^s}(1) is a very ample, hence ample, line bundle on X defined over F_{q^m}. Put q_0 = q^m. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_306 to q_0, X, and L. It gives integers r >= 1 and n >= 1 and a section s of the n-th tensor power of L on X_{F_{q_0^r}} whose zero scheme Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X_{F_{q_0^r}}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension 1 over F_{q_0^r}. Put Q = q_0^r = q^{m r}. The divisor Y is nonempty: if the zero scheme of an effective Cartier divisor were empty, the divisor would be zero, and the zero divisor is not ample on a positive-dimensional projective variety. As a closed subscheme of the projective surface X_{F_Q}, Y is projective; by the cited lemma it is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension 1, hence Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_Q. Next, by Miner/16d24b0281973336/04aee4 applied with base prime power q_0 and exponent r to the curve Y, the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius S on W = H^1_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is semisimple. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, S is diagonalizable over Q_ellbar. Now let i: Y -> X_{F_Q}. Identifying H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell) with H^1_et((X_{F_Q})_k, Q_ell) in the canonical way, by eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc with q = q_0, m = r, and d = 2, the restriction i^*: H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^1_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is injective and equivariant for the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let T_Q be the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on V. Then i^* T_Q = S i^*. Set U = im(i^*) in W. The subspace U is S-stable. Since S is diagonalizable over Q_ellbar, its restriction to U is diagonalizable over Q_ellbar: after base change to K = Q_ellbar, W_K is a direct sum of eigenspaces W_lambda for the distinct eigenvalues lambda of S, and the projection onto W_lambda is the polynomial product over mu != lambda of (S - mu)/(lambda - mu), hence preserves U_K; therefore U_K is the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_K intersection W_lambda. Because i^* is injective and T_Q-equivariant, V_K is isomorphic to U_K as a vector space with T_Q tensor 1 acting as S|_U tensor 1, so T_Q tensor 1 is diagonalizable over K. It remains to descend from Q to q^m. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a and functoriality of pullback, arithmetic Frobenius is pullback by the field automorphism c -> c^{q^m}; since c -> c^Q is the r-th power of c -> c^{q^m}, we have T_Q = F_m^r. Also F_m is invertible by the same lemma. We use the following linear-algebra fact: if A is an invertible linear operator on a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space and A^r is diagonalizable over K = Q_ellbar, then A is diagonalizable over K. Suppose A is not diagonalizable over K. Then over K, A has a nontrivial Jordan block for some eigenvalue lambda. Since A is invertible, lambda is nonzero. Let W be the lambda-generalized eigenspace of A. Then W is A^r-stable, and on W we have A = lambda(I+N) with N a nonzero nilpotent operator. Hence A^r|_W = lambda^r (I+N)^r. The operator (I+N)^r is unipotent. If it were the identity, then the minimal polynomial of I+N would divide both (t - 1)^d and t^r - 1, where d = dim_K W, and these polynomials have greatest common divisor t - 1 because the derivative of t^r - 1 at 1 is r, which is nonzero in characteristic 0; hence I+N would be the identity, contradicting N != 0. Thus (I+N)^r is a unipotent operator not equal to the identity, so it is not diagonalizable, because a diagonalizable unipotent operator has only the eigenvalue 1 and hence is the identity. Therefore A^r|_W is not diagonalizable, contradicting the fact already proved that a diagonalizable operator restricts to a diagonalizable operator on any invariant subspace. Hence A is diagonalizable over K. Applying this fact to A = F_m gives that F_m is diagonalizable over Q_ellbar. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let Y be a smooth ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m} that is geometrically connected, and let i:Y->X be the inclusion. Then for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-2, the restriction map i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is surjective.
proof: Let n be an integer with 0 <= n <= d-2. We prove that the restriction map i^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is surjective by applying the proved lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc. That lemma states that, under the same base-field and dimension assumptions, if X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 2 over F_{q^m} and Y is a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, then the restriction map i^* is an isomorphism for every n <= d-2 and is injective for n = d-1. We now check that the present Y satisfies the hypotheses of that lemma. The hypotheses on q, ell, m, k, d, and X are exactly as in the cited lemma. Since X is smooth, it is regular, so every divisor on X is an effective Cartier divisor; in particular the given divisor Y is an effective Cartier divisor. It is smooth and ample by hypothesis. It is nonempty: a smooth divisor on a smooth d-dimensional variety has pure dimension d-1, and d-1 >= 1 because d >= 2; equivalently, an ample effective divisor cannot have empty support. The additional hypothesis in the target statement that Y is geometrically connected is compatible with the cited lemma and is not needed for its conclusion. Therefore the cited lemma applies, and it gives that i^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every n <= d-2. Since our chosen n satisfies 0 <= n <= d-2, the map in degree n is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces. Every isomorphism is in particular surjective. Hence i^* is surjective for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d-2.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 2 over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, and let k be the algebraic closure of F_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 2 over F_{q^m}. Put Q=q^m. Since X is projective over F_Q, it admits a closed immersion into some projective space over F_Q, and the restriction of O(1) is an ample line bundle A on X defined over F_Q. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_306, applied to the prime power Q with this ample line bundle A, there exist integers r>=1 and n>=1 and a section s of the n-th tensor power of A on X_{F_{Q^r}} whose zero scheme Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X_{F_{Q^r}}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension 1. Let M=m r. Then X_M:=X_{F_{q^M}} is smooth, projective, and geometrically connected of dimension 2 over F_{q^M}, and Y is a smooth geometrically connected ample Cartier divisor on X_M. As a closed subscheme of the projective scheme X_M, Y is projective; together with smoothness, geometric connectedness, and dimension 1, this makes Y a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^M}. Let i:Y -> X_M be the closed immersion. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/f80cb4 with d=2 and with the base field F_{q^M}, the restriction map i^*:H^1_et(X_{M,k},Q_ell) -> H^1_et(Y_{M,k},Q_ell) is injective. The geometric fibers satisfy X_{M,k}=X_k and Y_{M,k}=Y_k, so after identifying V=H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) and W=H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell), we have an injective Q_ell-linear map i^*:V -> W. Let sigma:F_q -> F_q be sigma(x)=x^q. Let T be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V, i.e. T=(id_{X_k} times Spec sigma^m)^*. Let S be the q^M-power arithmetic Frobenius on W, i.e. S=(id_{Y_k} times Spec sigma^M)^*. Since M=m r, the q^M-power arithmetic Frobenius on V is T^r. Functoriality of pullback for the closed immersion i gives i^* o T^r = S o i^*. Therefore the image U=i^*(V) is an S-stable Q_ell-subspace of W, and under the Q_ell-linear isomorphism V -> U induced by i^*, the operator T^r corresponds to S|_U. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/04aee4 applied to the curve Y over F_{q^M}, S is semisimple on W. To make the equivalence with diagonalizability explicit, let K be the algebraic closure of Q_ell. Semisimplicity of S over Q_ell means that the minimal polynomial of S has no repeated irreducible factor; over K this polynomial splits into distinct linear factors, so S_K is diagonalizable on W_K. Because U is S-stable, U_K is S_K-stable. Since S_K is diagonalizable, W_K is the direct sum of its eigenspaces W_K = direct sum_{lambda in K} E_lambda. The eigenspace projections are polynomials in S_K, because the distinct eigenvalues give Lagrange interpolation polynomials, hence they preserve U_K. Thus U_K = direct sum_{lambda} (U_K intersection E_lambda), and S|_U is diagonalizable over K. Consequently T^r is diagonalizable over K on V_K. It remains to remove the power r. The Frobenius T is invertible, since it is induced by the automorphism sigma^m of the base field. Work over K. By the multiplicative Jordan-Chevalley decomposition for invertible operators, T = S_0 U, where S_0 is semisimple, U is unipotent, and S_0 U = U S_0. Then T^r = S_0^r U^r is a commuting product of a semisimple operator and a unipotent operator, hence it is the multiplicative Jordan-Chevalley decomposition of the invertible operator T^r. Since T^r is diagonalizable, its unipotent part is the identity, so U^r=1. If U != 1, its minimal polynomial is (t-1)^e for some e>1, while U^r=1 implies that the same minimal polynomial divides t^r-1. In characteristic 0 the greatest common divisor of (t-1)^e and t^r-1 is t-1, because t^r-1 has simple roots and its only common root with (t-1)^e is 1; this is a contradiction. Hence U=1, so T=S_0 is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over K. Thus the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius T is diagonalizable over the algebraic closure of Q_ell on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell).

statement: Let K be a field, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V) be diagonalizable over Kbar, and let W be a T-stable K-subspace of V. Then T|_W is diagonalizable over Kbar.
proof:
Let K be a field, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V) be diagonalizable over Kbar, and let W be a T-stable K-subspace of V. We prove that T|_W is diagonalizable over Kbar.

Write V_{Kbar} := V tensor_K Kbar, W_{Kbar} := W tensor_K Kbar, and T_{Kbar} := T tensor_K Id_{Kbar} in End_{Kbar}(V_{Kbar}).

Step 1 (W_{Kbar} is a T_{Kbar}-stable subspace of V_{Kbar}). The inclusion W -> V is injective. Since Kbar is a free, hence flat, K-module, tensoring preserves injectivity, so W_{Kbar} -> V_{Kbar} is injective; we identify W_{Kbar} with its image, a Kbar-linear subspace of V_{Kbar}. For w in W, T_{Kbar}(w tensor 1) = (Tw) tensor 1 lies in W_{Kbar} because W is T-stable. As W_{Kbar} is the Kbar-span of {w tensor 1 : w in W}, it follows that T_{Kbar}(W_{Kbar}) is contained in W_{Kbar}.

Step 2 (eigenspace decomposition of V_{Kbar}). By hypothesis T_{Kbar} is diagonalizable over Kbar. Hence there is a finite set Lambda subset Kbar such that V_{Kbar} = (direct sum over lambda in Lambda) E_lambda, where E_lambda := ker(T_{Kbar} - lambda Id_{V_{Kbar}}), and T_{Kbar}|_{E_lambda} = lambda Id_{E_lambda} for every lambda in Lambda. (If V = 0, take Lambda = empty; then W = 0 and the conclusion is the trivial statement that the zero operator on the zero space is diagonalizable, so assume V != 0 below, though the argument is uniform.)

Step 3 (the projections onto the eigenspaces are polynomials in T_{Kbar}). For lambda in Lambda, define pi_lambda := (product over mu in Lambda, mu != lambda) (T_{Kbar} - mu Id_{V_{Kbar}})/(lambda - mu), with the empty product equal to Id_{V_{Kbar}} when |Lambda| = 1. This is an element of Kbar[T_{Kbar}], a polynomial in T_{Kbar} with coefficients in Kbar. We claim pi_lambda is the projection of V_{Kbar} onto E_lambda along (direct sum over mu != lambda) E_mu. Indeed, let x in E_nu for some nu in Lambda; then T_{Kbar} x = nu x, so pi_lambda(x) = (product over mu != lambda) ((nu - mu)/(lambda - mu)) x. If nu = lambda this product is 1, giving pi_lambda(x) = x. If nu != lambda, the factor with mu = nu equals (nu - nu)/(lambda - nu) = 0, giving pi_lambda(x) = 0. Since the subspaces E_nu (nu in Lambda) span V_{Kbar}, pi_lambda acts as Id on E_lambda and as 0 on every E_nu with nu != lambda; hence pi_lambda is the claimed projection, and in particular pi_lambda lies in Kbar[T_{Kbar}].

Step 4 (W_{Kbar} is the direct sum of its intersections with the eigenspaces). Because pi_lambda is a polynomial in T_{Kbar} and W_{Kbar} is T_{Kbar}-stable, we have pi_lambda(W_{Kbar}) contained in W_{Kbar} for every lambda in Lambda (a T_{Kbar}-stable subspace is stable under every polynomial in T_{Kbar}). For w in W_{Kbar}, w = (sum over lambda in Lambda) pi_lambda(w), with each pi_lambda(w) in W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda; hence W_{Kbar} = (sum over lambda) (W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda). The sum is direct: if (sum over lambda) w_lambda = 0 with w_lambda in W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda, a fortiori w_lambda in E_lambda, then the directness of V_{Kbar} = (direct sum over lambda) E_lambda forces w_lambda = 0 for all lambda. Therefore W_{Kbar} = (direct sum over lambda in Lambda) (W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda).

Step 5 (T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}} is diagonalizable). For each lambda in Lambda, the subspace W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda is contained in E_lambda, on which T_{Kbar} acts as lambda Id. Hence every vector of W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda is an eigenvector of T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}} with eigenvalue lambda, i.e. W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda is contained in ker((T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}}) - lambda Id_{W_{Kbar}}). By Step 4, W_{Kbar} is the direct sum of the subspaces W_{Kbar} intersect E_lambda, each of which lies inside an eigenspace of T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}}. Thus W_{Kbar} is spanned by eigenvectors of T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}} (indeed it is a direct sum of eigenspaces), so T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}} is diagonalizable over Kbar.

Step 6 (conclusion). By construction, T_{Kbar}|_{W_{Kbar}} = (T|_W) tensor_K Id_{Kbar}, the extension of scalars of T|_W. Since this operator is diagonalizable over Kbar, the operator T|_W is diagonalizable over Kbar, as required.

(Equivalently, in minimal-polynomial terms: T diagonalizable over Kbar means the minimal polynomial m_T of T over K splits over Kbar into distinct linear factors; since W is T-stable, the minimal polynomial of T|_W over K divides m_T, hence also splits over Kbar into distinct linear factors, so T|_W is diagonalizable over Kbar. The eigenspace argument above gives the same conclusion directly and handles all edge cases, including V = 0, W = 0, and |Lambda| = 1.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), identify Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d. For 0<=s<=d put P^s=ker(L^{d-s+1}:H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-s+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), and let tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace. Then for every integer r with 0<=r<=d and every integer j with 0<=2j<=r, the bilinear form (x,y)->tr_X(x cup y) on L^j P^{r-2j} x L^{d-r+j} P^{r-2j} is nondegenerate.
proof: Let r' = r - 2j. Since 0 <= 2j <= r <= d, we have 0 <= r' <= d. Put P = P^{r'}. The hypothesis gives hard Lefschetz for L on X. By the proved lemma 'Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_542', the pairing beta(u,v) = tr_X(L^{d-r'}u cup v) is perfect on P x P, where tr_X is the Poincare duality trace; the normalization used in the cited lemma is the standard one, and if the trace in the statement is taken with another nonzero normalization, the pairing is multiplied by a nonzero scalar, which does not change nondegeneracy. Now let a be in L^j P and b be in L^{d-r+j} P. Write a = L^j u and b = L^{d-r+j} v with u,v in P. By definition L^n w = xi^n cup w. The cup product is associative and graded-commutative; since xi has degree 2, no sign appears when moving the xi-factors. Hence tr_X(a cup b) = tr_X((xi^j cup u) cup (xi^{d-r+j} cup v)) = tr_X(xi^{d-r+2j} cup (u cup v)) = tr_X(L^{d-r+2j} u cup v) = beta(u,v), because d-r' = d-r+2j. The formula is independent of the choice of preimages: if L^j u = L^j u', then beta(u-u',v)=0 for all v, so u=u'; similarly for L^{d-r+j}. Thus the stated pairing B is the pullback of the perfect pairing beta along the surjective maps L^j:P -> L^j P and L^{d-r+j}:P -> L^{d-r+j} P. To verify nondegeneracy directly, suppose a in L^j P satisfies B(a,b)=0 for every b in L^{d-r+j} P. Choose u in P with a = L^j u. For every v in P, taking b = L^{d-r+j}v gives 0 = B(a,b) = beta(u,v). Since beta is perfect, u = 0, so a = L^j u = 0. Similarly, if b in L^{d-r+j} P satisfies B(a,b)=0 for every a in L^j P, choose v in P with b = L^{d-r+j}v; then beta(u,v)=0 for every u in P, so v=0 and b=0. Therefore the left and right radicals of B are both zero, so B is nondegenerate. This argument covers all edge cases, including r=0 (where j=0 and P=P^0) and r=d (where r' can be d when j=0).

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), identify Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, and let L be cup product with xi. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-1. For 0<=s<=d put P^s=ker(L^{d-s+1}:H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-s+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), and put P^s=0 for s<0. Then for every integer r with 0<=r<d, the map from direct sum_{j>=0} L^j P^{r-2j} to H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) given by summing the images of L^j is an isomorphism.
proof: Let V^n = H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) for every integer n, with the standard convention V^n = 0 if n < 0 or n > 2d; this uses the usual vanishing of etale cohomology of a d-dimensional smooth projective variety outside the range 0 to 2d, and each V^n is finite dimensional. The operator L: V^n -> V^{n+2} is cup product with xi. By hypothesis L^{d-n}: V^n -> V^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0 <= n <= d-1; for n = d it is the identity, so the same statement holds for all 0 <= n <= d. For 0 <= s <= d put P^s = ker(L^{d-s+1}: V^s -> V^{2d-s+2}), and P^s = 0 for s < 0. Write a_n = dim V^n, with a_n = 0 for n < 0 or n > 2d. First compute dim P^n. For n = 0, the map L^{d+1}: V^0 -> V^{2d+2} is the zero map because V^{2d+2}=0, so P^0 = V^0 and dim P^0 = a_0. For n = 1, the map L^d: V^1 -> V^{2d+1} is the zero map because V^{2d+1}=0, so P^1 = V^1 and dim P^1 = a_1. Now let 2 <= n <= d. Hard Lefschetz in degree n-2 gives an isomorphism L^{d-n+2}: V^{n-2} -> V^{2d-n+2}. Hence dim V^{2d-n+2} = dim V^{n-2} = a_{n-2}. Also L^{d-n+1}: V^n -> V^{2d-n+2} is surjective: given z in V^{2d-n+2}, choose x in V^{n-2} with L^{d-n+2}x = z; then z = L^{d-n+1}(Lx). Therefore rank(L^{d-n+1}) = dim V^{2d-n+2} = a_{n-2}. Since P^n is the kernel of L^{d-n+1}, dim P^n = a_n - a_{n-2}. Thus for every 0 <= n <= d we have dim P^n = a_n - a_{n-2}, where a_{n-2}=0 if n<2. Fix r with 0 <= r < d and put N = floor(r/2). Only the indices j = 0, ..., N have r-2j >= 0, so the direct sum in the statement is finite. Define Phi: direct sum_{j=0}^N P^{r-2j} -> V^r by Phi(x_0, ..., x_N) = sum_{j=0}^N L^j x_j. We first note that L^j: P^{r-2j} -> V^r is injective. Indeed, let n = r-2j and suppose x in P^n satisfies L^j x = 0. Since r < d, d-r+j >= 1, so d-n-j = d-r+j is a nonnegative integer, and L^{d-n}x = L^{d-n-j} L^j x = 0. But n = r-2j <= r < d, so hard Lefschetz gives L^{d-n}: V^n -> V^{2d-n} as an isomorphism, hence x = 0. Therefore L^j identifies P^{r-2j} with the subspace L^j P^{r-2j} of V^r, and the map in the statement is the same as Phi under this identification. By the dimension formula, dim P^{r-2j} = a_{r-2j} - a_{r-2j-2}. Hence dim of the domain of Phi is sum_{j=0}^N (a_{r-2j} - a_{r-2j-2}) = a_r - a_{r-2N-2}. Since r-2N is 0 or 1, r-2N-2 is negative, so a_{r-2N-2}=0. Thus dim domain = a_r = dim V^r. It remains to prove that Phi is injective. Suppose Phi(x_0, ..., x_N) = 0. We prove by descending induction on M from N to 0 that x_M = 0. Assume x_{M+1}, ..., x_N have already been shown to be zero, so sum_{i=0}^M L^i x_i = 0. Apply L^{d-r+M} to this equality. For i < M, the i-th term becomes L^{d-r+M+i} x_i. Because x_i in P^{r-2i}, we have L^{d-r+2i+1} x_i = 0. Now d-r+M+i = (d-r+2i+1) + (M-i-1), and M-i-1 >= 0, so the i-th term is zero. The M-th term becomes L^{d-r+2M} x_M = L^{d-(r-2M)} x_M. Hence 0 = L^{d-(r-2M)} x_M. The integer r-2M satisfies 0 <= r-2M < d, so hard Lefschetz gives L^{d-(r-2M)}: V^{r-2M} -> V^{2d-r+2M} as an isomorphism, in particular injective. Therefore x_M = 0. This completes the induction. Thus Phi is injective. Since its domain and codomain have the same finite dimension, Phi is an isomorphism. Because each L^j identifies P^{r-2j} with L^j P^{r-2j}, the map from direct sum_{j>=0} L^j P^{r-2j} to H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) given by summing is an isomorphism. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. Fix 0<=r<d, put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), and let tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace. Then the bilinear form beta_r(x,y)=tr_X(x cup L^{d-r}y) on P^r is nondegenerate.
proof:
We prove that beta_r is nondegenerate on P^r. Throughout, H^n means H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell), and we use the standard fact that H^n=0 for n>2d (cohomological dimension of a smooth variety of dimension d is 2d), together with the associativity and graded commutativity of the cup product.

Step 1. A perfect pairing on H^r x H^{2d-r}.
By lemma_77(a), the canonical Poincare duality isomorphism tr_0: H^{2d} -> Q_ell(-d) is an isomorphism; in particular H^{2d} is one-dimensional over Q_ell. Fix an isomorphism psi: Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell (equivalently, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(d)); this is the standard identification of the Tate twist Q_ell(-d) with Q_ell. The map tr_X in the statement is the Poincare duality trace, hence a nonzero linear functional on the one-dimensional space H^{2d}. The map tr_0' := psi o tr_0: H^{2d} -> Q_ell is also a nonzero linear functional. Since the Q_ell-vector space of linear functionals on a one-dimensional space is itself one-dimensional, tr_X = c * tr_0' for some c in Q_ell^x.
By lemma_77(b), the pairing (u,v) -> tr_0(u cup v): H^r x H^{2d-r} -> Q_ell(-d) is a perfect pairing. Composing with the isomorphism psi: Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell, the pairing (u,v) -> psi(tr_0(u cup v)) is a perfect pairing into Q_ell; multiplying by the nonzero scalar c, the pairing
  <u,v> := tr_X(u cup v): H^r x H^{2d-r} -> Q_ell
is a perfect pairing (a nonzero scalar multiple of a perfect pairing is perfect).

Step 2. Reduction to an orthogonal complement.
For x,y in P^r, beta_r(x,y) = tr_X(x cup L^{d-r}y) = <x, L^{d-r}y>.
By hard Lefschetz with n=r (valid since 0<=r<d), the map L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{2d-r} is an isomorphism. Set W := L^{d-r}(P^r) subset H^{2d-r}. Since L^{d-r} is an isomorphism, y -> L^{d-r}y is a bijection P^r -> W, and dim W = dim P^r.
Define the left orthogonal
  W^perp := { u in H^r : <u,w> = 0 for every w in W }.
By perfectness of <.,.>, dim W^perp = dim H^r - dim W = dim H^r - dim P^r.
The left radical of beta_r is
  { x in P^r : beta_r(x,y)=0 for all y in P^r }
  = { x in P^r : <x, L^{d-r}y> = 0 for all y in P^r }
  = { x in P^r : <x,w> = 0 for all w in W }
  = P^r cap W^perp.
Hence beta_r is left nondegenerate if and only if P^r cap W^perp = 0. Because P^r is finite-dimensional over Q_ell, a bilinear form on P^r is nondegenerate if and only if it is left nondegenerate (the map P^r -> (P^r)^*, x -> (y -> beta_r(x,y)), is injective, hence bijective). It therefore suffices to prove P^r cap W^perp = 0.

Step 3. The case r < 2.
If r=0 or r=1, then 2d-r+2 > 2d, so H^{2d-r+2} = 0, and hence L^{d-r+1}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2} is the zero map; thus P^r = H^r. Then W = L^{d-r}(P^r) = L^{d-r}(H^r) = H^{2d-r} (as L^{d-r} is an isomorphism). Since W is all of H^{2d-r}, perfectness gives W^perp = 0. Therefore P^r cap W^perp = H^r cap 0 = 0.

Step 4. The case r >= 2.
Now 0 <= r-2 < d, so hard Lefschetz applies with n=r-2: the map L^{d-r+2}: H^{r-2} -> H^{2d-r+2} is an isomorphism.

(4a) L H^{r-2} subset W^perp. Let u = Lz in L H^{r-2} with z in H^{r-2}, and let w = L^{d-r}y in W with y in P^r. By associativity of the cup product,
  (Lz) cup (L^{d-r}y) = (xi cup z) cup (xi^{d-r} cup y) = xi cup z cup xi^{d-r} cup y.
Since xi has degree 2, graded commutativity gives xi cup z = (-1)^{2(r-2)} z cup xi = z cup xi (the exponent 2(r-2) is even). Hence
  (Lz) cup (L^{d-r}y) = z cup xi cup xi^{d-r} cup y = z cup xi^{d-r+1} cup y = z cup L^{d-r+1} y.
But y in P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}), so L^{d-r+1} y = 0, and therefore (Lz) cup (L^{d-r}y) = 0. Thus <u,w> = tr_X(0) = 0. As w was arbitrary in W, u in W^perp. Hence L H^{r-2} subset W^perp.

(4b) dim L H^{r-2} = dim W^perp.
First, L: H^{r-2} -> H^r is injective: indeed L^{d-r+2} = L^{d-r+1} o L is an isomorphism (hence injective), so L is injective; thus dim L H^{r-2} = dim H^{r-2}.
Next, L^{d-r+1}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2} is surjective: since L^{d-r+2} = L^{d-r+1} o L is an isomorphism, it is surjective, so im(L^{d-r+1}) contains im(L^{d-r+2}) = H^{2d-r+2}. Hence rank(L^{d-r+1}) = dim H^{2d-r+2}. As L^{d-r+2}: H^{r-2} -> H^{2d-r+2} is an isomorphism, dim H^{2d-r+2} = dim H^{r-2}, so rank(L^{d-r+1}) = dim H^{r-2}. Therefore
  dim P^r = dim ker(L^{d-r+1}) = dim H^r - rank(L^{d-r+1}) = dim H^r - dim H^{r-2}.
Combining with dim W^perp = dim H^r - dim P^r (Step 2) and dim W = dim P^r:
  dim W^perp = dim H^r - dim P^r = dim H^r - (dim H^r - dim H^{r-2}) = dim H^{r-2} = dim L H^{r-2}.
Since L H^{r-2} subset W^perp and the two subspaces of H^r have equal finite dimension, L H^{r-2} = W^perp.

(4c) P^r cap L H^{r-2} = 0. Let x in P^r cap L H^{r-2}. Then x = Lz for some z in H^{r-2}, and L^{d-r+1} x = 0 (as x in P^r). Hence 0 = L^{d-r+1} x = L^{d-r+1}(Lz) = L^{d-r+2} z. Since L^{d-r+2} is an isomorphism, z = 0, so x = 0.

(4d) From (4b) and (4c), P^r cap W^perp = P^r cap L H^{r-2} = 0.

Step 5. Conclusion.
In both cases (r<2 in Step 3, r>=2 in Step 4) we have P^r cap W^perp = 0, so the left radical of beta_r is trivial; beta_r is left nondegenerate. As P^r is finite-dimensional, beta_r is nondegenerate.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)), and let tr_Y:H^{2d}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace. Then the Q_ell-bilinear form beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r} y) is nondegenerate on P^r.
proof:
I have all I need. The proof is a direct corollary of `Miner/16d24b0281973336/4b7666` with j=0, which uses the same Poincaré trace and the same definition of P^r as the target, so no normalization or transpose adjustment is required. The argument is uniform in r (covering the edge cases r=0 and r=d) and relies only on the fact that L^{d-r} restricts to an isomorphism P^r → L^{d-r}P^r.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/cdaa8e",
  "cited_lemmas": ["Miner/16d24b0281973336/4b7666"],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that the Q_ell-bilinear form beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y) is nondegenerate on P^r, i.e. we establish both: (1) if x in P^r satisfies beta_r(x,y)=0 for every y in P^r, then x=0; and (2) if y in P^r satisfies beta_r(x,y)=0 for every x in P^r, then y=0.

Step 1 (L^{d-r} is an isomorphism, hence injective). By the hypothesis of the lemma, for every integer n with 0<=n<=d the map L^{d-n}:H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. Since 0<=r<=d, taking n=r gives that L^{d-r}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. In particular L^{d-r} is injective.

Step 2 (T is an isomorphism). Let L^{d-r}P^r := {L^{d-r}y : y in P^r} (a subspace of H^{2d-r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)) denote the image of P^r under L^{d-r}, and define T:P^r->L^{d-r}P^r by T(y)=L^{d-r}y. Surjectivity: by the definition of L^{d-r}P^r as the set of all elements L^{d-r}y with y in P^r, every element of L^{d-r}P^r equals T(y) for some y in P^r, so T is surjective. Injectivity: if T(y)=0, i.e. L^{d-r}y=0, then since L^{d-r}:H^r->H^{2d-r} is injective (Step 1) and y in H^r, we get y=0, so T is injective. Hence T:P^r->L^{d-r}P^r is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces.

Step 3 (nondegeneracy of the Poincare pairing on P^r x L^{d-r}P^r). Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/4b7666 to the variety Y (in place of its X), with the same q, ell, m, k, d, xi, L, tr_Y and the same definition P^s=ker(L^{d-s+1}:H^s->H^{2d-s+2}). The hypotheses of 4b7666 are exactly the hypotheses of the present lemma (in particular the hard Lefschetz assumption that L^{d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d). Taking the integer j=0 (which satisfies 0<=2j=0<=r), 4b7666 asserts that the bilinear form B(x,w):=tr_Y(x cup w) is nondegenerate on P^r x L^{d-r}P^r. Concretely this means: (3a) if x in P^r and B(x,w)=0 for every w in L^{d-r}P^r, then x=0; and (3b) if w in L^{d-r}P^r and B(x,w)=0 for every x in P^r, then w=0. (The form B is well-defined because for x in P^r subset H^r and w in L^{d-r}P^r subset H^{2d-r}, the cup product x cup w lies in H^{2d}, on which tr_Y is defined.)

Step 4 (relate beta_r to B). For x in P^r and y in P^r, beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y)=B(x,T(y)), using the definition of T in Step 2.

Step 5 (prove (1)). Let x in P^r with beta_r(x,y)=0 for every y in P^r. Then B(x,T(y))=0 for every y in P^r. Since T:P^r->L^{d-r}P^r is surjective (Step 2), for every w in L^{d-r}P^r there exists y in P^r with T(y)=w; hence B(x,w)=0 for every w in L^{d-r}P^r. By (3a), x=0. This proves (1).

Step 6 (prove (2)). Let y in P^r with beta_r(x,y)=0 for every x in P^r. Set w:=T(y) in L^{d-r}P^r. Then for every x in P^r, B(x,w)=B(x,T(y))=beta_r(x,y)=0. By (3b), w=0, i.e. T(y)=0. Since T is injective (Step 2), y=0. This proves (2).

Conclusion. From (1) and (2), the Q_ell-bilinear form beta_r(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup L^{d-r}y) is nondegenerate on P^r. The argument is uniform in r and in particular covers the boundary cases: for r=0 one has P^0=ker(L^{d+1})=H^0 and L^dP^0=H^{2d}, so Step 3 with j=0 is the usual Poincare duality nondegeneracy on H^0 x H^{2d}; for r=d one has P^d=ker(L) and L^0P^d=P^d, so beta_d(x,y)=tr_Y(x cup y) is exactly the pairing of Step 3. This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=1, and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)) and Q^r=ker(L:H^{2d-r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)). Then L^{d-r}:P^r->Q^r is an isomorphism.
proof:
The search confirms no listed lemma is needed: this statement is purely linear algebra over the Hard Lefschetz hypothesis already built into the lemma's own assumptions. I will write the proof following the well-typed route: (1) $L^{d-r}(P^r) \subseteq \ker(L)$, (2) injectivity from the Hard Lefschetz isomorphism $L^{d-r}: H^r 	o H^{2d-r}$, (3) surjectivity by lifting any $y \in \ker(L) \subseteq H^{2d-r}$ uniquely to $x \in H^r$, which then lies in $P^r$ because $L^{d-r+1}x = Ly = 0$.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/c671d8",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Fix an integer r with 0 <= r <= d. Write H^n = H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) for brevity. Recall the definitions: P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2}) and Q^r = ker(L: H^{2d-r} -> H^{2d-r+2}). The standing hypothesis is that for every n with 0 <= n <= d, the map L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism.

Step 0 (degree bookkeeping; well-typedness). Since xi is the cycle class of a divisor (codimension 1), cup product with xi, i.e. L, raises cohomological degree by 2. Hence L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{r+2(d-r)} = H^{2d-r}, and L^{d-r+1} = L o L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2}. Thus P^r is a Q_ell-subspace of H^r (kernel of a linear map), Q^r is a Q_ell-subspace of H^{2d-r} (kernel of a linear map), and L^{d-r} restricts to a linear map from P^r into H^{2d-r}.

Step 1 (L^{d-r}(P^r) is contained in Q^r, so L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r is well-defined). Let x be in P^r. By definition of P^r, L^{d-r+1}x = 0. Since L^{d-r+1} = L o L^{d-r} (composition of the linear map L with itself, by the definition of powers of a linear operator), this reads L(L^{d-r}x) = 0. The element L^{d-r}x lies in H^{2d-r} by Step 0, so L^{d-r}x lies in ker(L: H^{2d-r} -> H^{2d-r+2}) = Q^r. Therefore L^{d-r}(P^r) is contained in Q^r, and L^{d-r} factors through a well-defined Q_ell-linear map L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r.

Step 2 (injectivity). By the standing hypothesis with n = r (valid since 0 <= r <= d), the map L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{2d-r} is an isomorphism, in particular injective. Its restriction to the subspace P^r of H^r is injective: indeed, if x is in P^r and L^{d-r}(x) = 0 in H^{2d-r}, then x = 0 because L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{2d-r} is injective. Now view the same restricted map with codomain Q^r (possible by Step 1). If x is in P^r and L^{d-r}(x) = 0 in Q^r, then a fortiori L^{d-r}(x) = 0 in H^{2d-r} (the zero element of Q^r is the zero element of H^{2d-r}), hence x = 0. Thus L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r is injective.

Step 3 (surjectivity). Let y be in Q^r. Then y is an element of H^{2d-r} with Ly = 0. By the standing hypothesis with n = r, L^{d-r}: H^r -> H^{2d-r} is an isomorphism, in particular surjective, so there exists a unique x in H^r with L^{d-r}(x) = y. Then L^{d-r+1}(x) = L(L^{d-r}(x)) = L(y) = 0, so x lies in P^r. Hence y = L^{d-r}(x) for some x in P^r, i.e. y is in L^{d-r}(P^r). Since y was arbitrary in Q^r, we get Q^r is contained in L^{d-r}(P^r); combined with Step 1 this gives L^{d-r}(P^r) = Q^r, so the map L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r is surjective.

Conclusion. By Steps 2 and 3, the Q_ell-linear map L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r is both injective and surjective. A linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces (indeed, between any vector spaces) that is injective and surjective is an isomorphism: its set-theoretic inverse is linear, since if f is linear and bijective, then f^{-1}(a+b) = f^{-1}(f(f^{-1}(a)) + f(f^{-1}(b))) = f^{-1}(a) + f^{-1}(b) and similarly for scalar multiples. Therefore L^{d-r}: P^r -> Q^r is an isomorphism.

Edge cases. The argument applies verbatim for every r with 0 <= r <= d. For r = d: L^{d-r} = L^0 = the identity on H^d, P^d = ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}) = Q^d, and the identity map P^d -> Q^d is trivially an isomorphism (Steps 1-3 reduce to tautologies: L^{d-r+1} = L, and the Hard Lefschetz map with n = d is L^0 = id: H^d -> H^d). For r = 0: P^0 = ker(L^{d+1}: H^0 -> H^{2d+2}), Q^0 = ker(L: H^{2d} -> H^{2d+2}), and L^d: P^0 -> Q^0 is shown an isomorphism by the same three steps using the Hard Lefschetz isomorphism L^d: H^0 -> H^{2d} (the n = 0 case). No separate treatment is needed; the general argument covers all cases.

No proved lemma or reference is invoked: the proof uses only the Hard Lefschetz hypothesis stated in the lemma, the degree-shift property of cup product with the divisor class xi, and elementary linear algebra (kernels of linear maps are subspaces; restriction of an injective map to a subspace is injective; a bijective linear map is an isomorphism)."
}

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m} that is geometrically connected, and let i:Y->X be the inclusion. Suppose i^*:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer r with 0<=r<=d-2 and is injective for r=d-1. Suppose that for every integer r with 0<=r<=d-1, every eigenvalue of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell) has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Then for every integer r with 0<=r<=d-1, every eigenvalue of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.
proof: Fix r with 0 <= r <= d-1. Put V = H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell), W = H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell), and a = i^*: V -> W. Let F_X and F_Y denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms on V and W. We first prove that a is Frobenius-equivariant. Let sigma: k -> k be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius of k, sigma(x)=x^q. For a variety Z over F_{q^m}, let phi_Z: Z_k -> Z_k be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism, i.e. the automorphism whose base component is sigma^m and whose Z component is id_Z; its pullback on etale cohomology is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(Z_k,Q_ell). Since i is defined over F_{q^m}, the base-changed inclusion i_k: Y_k -> X_k satisfies phi_X o i_k = i_k o phi_Y, because both composites are the morphism Y_k -> X_k obtained from i by applying sigma^m to the base factor. By functoriality of pullback in etale cohomology, (phi_X o i_k)^* = i_k^* o phi_X^* and (i_k o phi_Y)^* = phi_Y^* o i_k^*. Hence a o F_X = F_Y o a. Tensoring this identity with overline(Q_ell), the extended map abar = a tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) satisfies abar o F_Xbar = F_Ybar o abar, where F_Xbar and F_Ybar are the extended Frobenius operators. The map a is injective for every r under consideration: it is an isomorphism when r <= d-2 and is injective when r = d-1. Tensoring an injective map of vector spaces over a field with a field extension preserves injectivity, so abar is injective. Let lambda be an eigenvalue of F_Xbar; then there is a nonzero v in Vbar with F_Xbar(v) = lambda v. Put w = abar(v). By injectivity of abar, w is nonzero. Using the equivariance identity, F_Ybar(w) = F_Ybar(abar(v)) = abar(F_Xbar(v)) = lambda abar(v) = lambda w. Thus lambda is an eigenvalue of F_Ybar. By the hypothesis applied to H^r_et(Y_k,Q_ell), every eigenvalue of F_Ybar has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Therefore lambda has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Since lambda was arbitrary, every eigenvalue of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. This completes the proof for the chosen r, and since r was arbitrary in 0 <= r <= d-1, the lemma follows.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let Y be a smooth ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m} that is geometrically connected, and let i:Y->X be the inclusion. Then for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-2, the restriction map i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective.
proof:
We prove the target statement as a direct corollary of the proved weak Lefschetz lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc.

That lemma asserts the following. Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=2 over F_{q^m}, let Y be a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let i:Y -> X be the closed immersion. Then the restriction map i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n<=d-2 (and injective for n=d-1).

We now verify that the hypotheses of the present lemma imply the hypotheses of eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc.

(1) Parameters. The parameters q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and d>=2 are exactly the same in the two statements.

(2) The variety X. By hypothesis of the present lemma, X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, which matches the hypothesis on X in eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc verbatim.

(3) The divisor Y. We show that Y is a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}.
   (a) Smooth: Y is a smooth divisor by hypothesis.
   (b) Ample: Y is ample by hypothesis.
   (c) Defined over F_{q^m}: Y is defined over F_{q^m} by hypothesis.
   (d) Cartier: X is smooth. A smooth divisor on a smooth variety is a smooth closed subscheme of pure codimension 1, so the closed immersion Y -> X is a regular immersion; equivalently, on the smooth variety X every divisor is a Cartier divisor. Hence Y is a Cartier divisor on X.
   (e) Nonempty: Y is geometrically connected by hypothesis, and a geometrically connected variety is in particular a nonempty variety. Independently, an ample divisor on a variety of dimension d>=2 is an effective Cartier divisor; if Y were empty then the associated line bundle O_X(Y) would be the trivial line bundle O_X, which is not ample when d>=2 (its top self-intersection on any curve would be 0), a contradiction. Hence Y is nonempty.
   Combining (a)-(e), Y is a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, as required by eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc.

(4) The map i. The inclusion i:Y -> X is precisely the closed immersion Y -> X.

Having verified all hypotheses, eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc applies and yields that for every integer n<=d-2 the restriction map i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism.

The present lemma asks for injectivity of i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-2. For each such n we have n<=d-2, so by the preceding paragraph the map i^* in degree n is an isomorphism, and in particular is injective. This proves the desired conclusion for every integer n with 0<=n<=d-2. QED

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}, let C be a smooth geometrically connected very ample curve on S defined over F_{q^m}, let i:C->S be the inclusion, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Q_ell(1) with Q_ell, let xi be the class of the cycle class of C in H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell), let L be cup product with xi, let tr_C:H^2_et(C_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace, and let W be the image of i^*:H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell)->H^1_et(C_k,Q_ell). Then the pairing (a,b)->tr_C(a cup b) restricted to W is nondegenerate if and only if L:H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell)->H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell) is injective.
proof:
We prove that the pairing (a,b) ↦ tr_C(a∪b) restricted to W×W is nondegenerate if and only if L: H¹(S_k)→H³(S_k) is injective.

Step 1 (i^* is injective, so W is canonically H¹(S_k)). By the lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/58bcf9, applied with d=2, X=S, and Y=C (a smooth geometrically connected very ample Cartier divisor on the smooth projective geometrically connected surface S), the restriction map i^*: H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ) → H¹(C_k,Q_ℓ) is injective. Hence i^* identifies H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ) canonically with W = im(i^*) ⊂ H¹(C_k,Q_ℓ); write φ: H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ) → W for this isomorphism, φ(x) = i^*x.

Step 2 (Transport the pairing to H¹(S_k)). Define B: H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ)×H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ) → Q_ℓ by B(x,y) = tr_C(φ(x)∪φ(y)) = tr_C(i^*x∪i^*y). We claim that the pairing (a,b)↦tr_C(a∪b) on W is nondegenerate if and only if B is nondegenerate. For the forward direction, suppose the W-pairing is nondegenerate and B is degenerate; then there exists x∈H¹(S_k) with B(x,·)=0, i.e. tr_C(φ(x)∪b)=0 for all b∈W. By nondegeneracy of the W-pairing, φ(x)=0, and since φ is injective, x=0, a contradiction. For the reverse direction, suppose B is nondegenerate and the W-pairing is degenerate; then there exists a∈W with tr_C(a∪b)=0 for all b∈W. Since φ is surjective onto W, a=φ(x) for some x∈H¹(S_k), so B(x,·)=0, hence x=0 by nondegeneracy of B, so a=0, a contradiction. This proves the claim.

Step 3 (Express B via the Gysin map). Let i_!: H¹(C_k,Q_ℓ)→H³(S_k,Q_ℓ) be the Gysin homomorphism characterized by tr_S(i_!a∪b) = tr_C(a∪i^*b) for all a∈H¹(C_k,Q_ℓ) and b∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ); this is precisely the defining property of i_! given in the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor with d=2 and n=1. Then for x,y∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ), taking a=i^*x and b=y in the defining identity gives B(x,y) = tr_C(i^*x∪i^*y) = tr_S(i_!i^*x∪y).

Step 4 (Projection formula). By the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor, applied with d=2, X=S, and Y=C (a smooth effective divisor of pure dimension 1 on the smooth projective geometrically connected surface S), we have i_!(i^*x) = x∪ξ for every x∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ). Since L is cup product with ξ, this reads i_!i^*x = Lx. Substituting into Step 3 yields B(x,y) = tr_S(Lx∪y) for all x,y∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ).

Step 5 (Poincaré duality on S). By the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, part (b), applied with d=2 and n=1 to the smooth projective geometrically connected surface S, the pairing (a,b)↦tr_S(a∪b): H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ)×H³(S_k,Q_ℓ)→Q_ℓ is a perfect (nondegenerate) pairing of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. In particular, for any fixed u∈H³(S_k,Q_ℓ), if tr_S(y∪u)=0 for every y∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ), then u=0.

Step 6 (Conclusion). For x∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ), we have the following chain of equivalences: B(x,·)=0 if and only if tr_S(Lx∪y)=0 for every y∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ) (by Step 4); this holds if and only if tr_S(y∪Lx)=0 for every y∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ), since the cup product is graded-commutative, (Lx)∪y = (−1)^{3·1} y∪(Lx) = −y∪(Lx), and the sign is irrelevant for vanishing; and this holds if and only if Lx=0 (by the nondegeneracy of the perfect pairing in Step 5, applied to u=Lx∈H³(S_k,Q_ℓ)). Hence B(x,·)=0 if and only if Lx=0 for every x∈H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ), which is to say that B is nondegenerate if and only if L: H¹(S_k,Q_ℓ)→H³(S_k,Q_ℓ) is injective. By Step 2, the pairing (a,b)↦tr_C(a∪b) restricted to W is nondegenerate if and only if B is nondegenerate. Therefore the pairing (a,b)↦tr_C(a∪b) restricted to W is nondegenerate if and only if L is injective. ∎

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline(F_q), and let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, and let L be cup product with xi. Then for every integer n with 0<=n<=1, the map L^{1-n}:H^n_et(C_k,Q_ell)->H^{2-n}_et(C_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism.
proof:
Set d=1. The case n=1 is immediate: L^{1-1}=L^0 is the identity endomorphism of H^1_et(C_k,Q_l), hence an isomorphism.

For n=0, we prove that L: H^0_et(C_k,Q_l) -> H^2_et(C_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism. We use the implicit identification of Q_l(1) with Q_l under which the cycle class xi is regarded as an element of H^2_et(C_k,Q_l).

Because C is geometrically connected, C_k is connected. The group H^0_et(C_k,Q_l) is the group of sections of the constant sheaf Q_l, i.e. the locally constant functions from the underlying topological space of C_k to Q_l. Connectedness forces every locally constant function to be constant, so H^0_et(C_k,Q_l) is canonically Q_l. Let 1 denote the constant function 1.
